lawAreas.title: Offside and onside in open play
Players on the ground in open play

questions.stem: What is the maximum length of the field of play, measured from try line to try line?
questions.explanation: The field of play can be no longer than 100 metres between the try lines, and no shorter than 94 metres.

questions.stem: What is the minimum length of the field of play, measured from try line to try line?
questions.explanation: The field of play must be at least 94 metres long. The longest it can be is 100 metres.

questions.stem: What is the maximum width of the playing area?
questions.explanation: The playing area can be up to 70 metres wide and must be at least 68 metres wide.

questions.stem: What is the minimum width of the playing area?
questions.explanation: The playing area must be at least 68 metres wide. The widest it can be is 70 metres.

questions.stem: What is the maximum length of an in-goal area, from the try line to the dead-ball line?
questions.explanation: Each in-goal can be between 6 and 22 metres long.

questions.stem: What is the minimum length of an in-goal area, from the try line to the dead-ball line?
questions.explanation: Each in-goal must be at least 6 metres long and can be as long as 22 metres.

questions.stem: A ground has try lines 97 metres apart and in-goal areas 8 metres long. How does it compare with the dimensions in law?

options.text: Both measurements are within the permitted range
The in-goal areas are too short
The field of play is too short
The field of play is too long

questions.explanation: A field of play may be 94 to 100 metres long and an in-goal 6 to 22 metres long, so both are acceptable.

questions.stem: A pitch is marked 66 metres wide. How does that compare with the dimensions in law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range
It is 2 metres wider than the maximum
It is 4 metres narrower than the minimum
It is 2 metres narrower than the minimum

questions.explanation: The playing area must be between 68 and 70 metres wide, so 66 metres is 2 metres short.

questions.stem: Measured from dead-ball line to dead-ball line, what is the greatest overall length a playing area can have?
questions.explanation: A 100-metre field of play with a 22-metre in-goal at each end gives 144 metres.

questions.stem: Measured from dead-ball line to dead-ball line, what is the shortest overall length a playing area can have?
questions.explanation: A 94-metre field of play with a 6-metre in-goal at each end gives 106 metres.

questions.stem: What shape must the playing area be?
questions.explanation: The law requires the playing area to be a rectangle.

questions.stem: A club's pitch does not match the dimensions in law. Who must approve it for a domestic competition?
questions.explanation: Variations to the dimensions need the approval of the union for domestic competitions, and of World Rugby for international matches.

questions.stem: A stadium's pitch does not match the dimensions in law. Who must approve it for an international match?
questions.explanation: For international matches, any variation to the dimensions has to be approved by World Rugby.

questions.stem: A field of play is only 96 metres long. Which marked distance is reduced to make the lines fit?

options.text: The distance between the 10-metre lines and the 22-metre lines
The distance between the try lines and the 5-metre lines
The distance between the try lines and the 22-metre lines
The distance between the half-way line and the 10-metre lines

questions.explanation: On a field shorter than 100 metres, it is the gap between the 10-metre and 22-metre lines that shrinks. The other line distances stay the same.

questions.stem: A playing area is only 68 metres wide. Which marked distance is reduced to make the lines fit?

options.text: The distance between the two goal posts
The distance between each touchline and its 15-metre line
The distance between the two 15-metre lines
The distance between each touchline and its 5-metre line

questions.explanation: On a pitch narrower than 70 metres, the gap between the two 15-metre lines shrinks. Each 15-metre line stays 15 metres from its touchline.

questions.stem: Where it is practicable, how wide should the perimeter area around the playing area be?
questions.explanation: The perimeter area should be five metres wide where that can be achieved.

questions.stem: What is the narrowest the perimeter area may be for a men's match?
questions.explanation: The perimeter should be 5 metres where practicable, but never less than 3.5 metres for the men's game.

questions.stem: What is the narrowest the perimeter area may be for a women's match?
questions.explanation: The perimeter should be 5 metres where practicable, but never less than 3 metres for the women's game.

questions.stem: Which of these lines is marked as a solid line?
questions.explanation: The 22-metre lines are solid. The 5-metre, 10-metre and 15-metre lines are all dash lines.

questions.stem: Which of these lines is marked as a dash line?
questions.explanation: The 10-metre lines are dash lines. The 22-metre lines, half-way line and try lines are solid.

questions.stem: How are the touch-in-goal lines marked?
questions.explanation: The touch-in-goal lines are solid, like the dead-ball lines, try lines and touchlines.

questions.stem: How long is each dash in a dash line?
questions.explanation: Every dash in a dash line is five metres long.

questions.stem: Two dash lines run parallel to each touchline. How far from the touchline is the nearer one?
questions.explanation: There is a dash line 5 metres in from each touchline, and another 15 metres in.

questions.stem: Two dash lines run parallel to each touchline. How far from the touchline is the farther one?
questions.explanation: There is a dash line 15 metres in from each touchline, and another 5 metres in.

questions.stem: A dash line runs across the field in front of each try line. How far from the try line is it?
questions.explanation: There is a dash line five metres from each try line and parallel to it.

questions.stem: A dash line runs across the field on each side of the half-way line. How far from the half-way line is it?
questions.explanation: The dash lines either side of half-way are each 10 metres from it.

questions.stem: How many dash lines run the length of the field, parallel to the touchlines?
questions.explanation: Each touchline has two: one 5 metres in and one 15 metres in. That makes four.

questions.stem: How far apart are the two 10-metre lines?
questions.explanation: Each 10-metre line is 10 metres from the half-way line, so they are 20 metres apart.

questions.stem: On one side of the pitch, how far is it from the 5-metre line to the 15-metre line?
questions.explanation: One line is 5 metres from the touchline and the other 15 metres, so the gap between them is 10 metres.

questions.stem: On a pitch 70 metres wide, how far apart are the two 15-metre lines?
questions.explanation: Each 15-metre line is 15 metres in from its touchline, which leaves 40 metres between them on a 70-metre pitch.

questions.stem: On a field of play 100 metres long, how far is it from a 22-metre line to the nearer 10-metre line?
questions.explanation: Half the field is 50 metres. Take away 22 metres to the 22-metre line and 10 metres back from half-way, and 18 metres remain.

questions.stem: How long is the short line that crosses the centre of the half-way line?
questions.explanation: A single line half a metre long crosses the middle of the half-way line.

questions.stem: Where on the ground is there a single line just half a metre long?

options.text: Where each 15-metre line meets the half-way line
Across the centre of each try line
Across the centre of each 22-metre line
Across the centre of the half-way line

questions.explanation: The only half-metre line is the one that crosses the centre of the half-way line.

questions.stem: How far apart are the two goal posts?
questions.explanation: The goal posts stand 5.6 metres apart.

questions.stem: How high above the ground is the top edge of the crossbar?
questions.explanation: The top edge of the crossbar is 3 metres from the ground.

questions.stem: What is the minimum height of the goal posts?
questions.explanation: The posts must be at least 3.4 metres high. The crossbar's top edge is at 3 metres.

questions.stem: When the goal posts are padded, how far from the try line may the outer edge of the padding be?
questions.explanation: The outside edge of any post padding must be within 0.3 metres of the try line.

questions.stem: How many flag posts with flags are there on the ground?
questions.explanation: There are 14: eight at the corners of the in-goal areas, and six beside the touchlines level with the 22-metre lines and the half-way line.

questions.stem: What is the minimum height of a flag post?
questions.explanation: Each flag post must be at least 1.2 metres high.

questions.stem: How many flag posts mark the corners of the two in-goal areas?
questions.explanation: There is one where each touch-in-goal line meets a try line and one where it meets a dead-ball line: four at each end, eight in all.

questions.stem: Where do flag posts stand along the touch-in-goal lines?

options.text: Only where they meet the try lines
Only where they meet the dead-ball lines
Where they meet the try lines and the dead-ball lines

questions.explanation: Each touch-in-goal line has a flag post at both ends: at the try line and at the dead-ball line.

questions.stem: How many flag posts stand level with the 22-metre lines and the half-way line?
questions.explanation: There is one on each side of the pitch level with each 22-metre line and with the half-way line, making six.

questions.stem: How far outside the touchline are the flag posts that stand level with the 22-metre lines and the half-way line?
questions.explanation: These six flag posts are placed two metres outside the touchlines.

questions.stem: The flag posts level with the half-way line stand outside the touchlines. Which area must they still be inside?
questions.explanation: They stand two metres outside the touchline, so they are outside the playing area, but they must be within the playing enclosure.

questions.stem: Which of these is a permitted playing surface?
questions.explanation: The permitted surfaces are grass, sand, clay, snow and artificial turf.

questions.stem: Besides grass and artificial turf, which group of surfaces does the law permit?
questions.explanation: The permitted surfaces are grass, sand, clay, snow and artificial turf. Gravel, cinder and ice are not on the list.

questions.stem: An artificial turf pitch is permitted provided it conforms to which World Rugby regulation?
questions.explanation: Artificial turf must meet World Rugby Regulation 22.

questions.stem: What is the one requirement the law makes of every playing surface?
questions.explanation: Whatever the surface is made of, it must be safe to play on.

questions.stem: A team is unhappy with the state of the ground. When must it tell the referee?

options.text: Within 24 hours of the final whistle
At the first stoppage in play

questions.explanation: Any objection to the ground has to be raised with the referee before the match begins.

questions.stem: A team objects to the ground before the match. What does the referee do first?

options.text: Starts play and reports the objection afterwards
Refers the objection to the home union

questions.explanation: The referee tries to sort out the problem. The match is not started only if part of the ground is judged unsafe.

questions.stem: Before kick-off the referee judges that part of the ground is unsafe and it cannot be put right. What should the referee do?

options.text: Start it and keep play away from that area
Start it and report the problem afterwards

questions.explanation: A referee will not start a match if any part of the ground is considered unsafe.

questions.stem: What does the playing area consist of?

options.text: The field of play and the two in-goal areas
The field of play, the in-goal areas and the perimeter area

questions.explanation: The playing area is the field of play plus both in-goal areas.

questions.stem: What does the playing enclosure consist of?

options.text: The field of play and the in-goal areas
The playing area and the spectator areas
The playing area and the perimeter area around it

questions.explanation: The playing enclosure is the playing area together with the perimeter area surrounding it.

questions.stem: Which of these lines is part of the in-goal area?
questions.explanation: In-goal includes the try line, but not the dead-ball line or the touch-in-goal lines.

questions.stem: Which of these lines is part of the playing area?
questions.explanation: The try line belongs to in-goal, which is part of the playing area. The touchlines, touch-in-goal lines and dead-ball lines are outside it.

questions.stem: The 22 runs from the try line to the 22-metre line. Which line is included in it?
questions.explanation: The 22 includes the 22-metre line itself, but not the try line or the touchlines.

questions.stem: Which area do the touchlines belong to?
questions.explanation: The touchlines are not part of the field of play. Touch is the area alongside the field of play and includes the touchlines.

questions.stem: Who must stay in the technical zone until they are required?

options.text: Only the team doctor and physiotherapist

questions.explanation: The technical zone is where replacements, water carriers and coaches wait until they are needed.

questions.stem: In a match played with squads of 23, who is allowed in the technical zone?
questions.explanation: When squads are 23 strong, the technical zone is for water carriers only.

questions.stem: In the ground diagram, how far from the touchline is each technical zone?
questions.explanation: The diagram shows each technical zone set two metres back from the touchline.

questions.stem: In the ground diagram, how long is each technical zone, measured along the touchline?
questions.explanation: The diagram shows each technical zone as 10 metres long and 3 metres deep.

questions.stem: How many panels is a rugby ball made of?
questions.explanation: The ball is oval and made of four panels.

questions.stem: What shape does the law require the ball to be?
questions.explanation: The law describes the ball as oval.

questions.stem: A manufacturer supplies a ball stitched from six panels. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It complies, because any even number of panels is allowed
It does not comply, because the ball must have two panels
It complies, because the law sets no number of panels
It does not comply, because the ball must have four panels

questions.explanation: The law specifies a ball made of four panels.

questions.stem: What is the minimum length of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball must be between 280 and 300 millimetres long.

questions.stem: What is the maximum length of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball must be between 280 and 300 millimetres long.

questions.stem: A ball measures 305 millimetres from end to end. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: The longest a ball may be is 300 millimetres, so 305 is 5 millimetres over.

questions.stem: A ball measures 275 millimetres from end to end. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: The shortest a ball may be is 280 millimetres, so 275 is 5 millimetres under.

questions.stem: Which measurement of the ball must be between 280 and 300 millimetres?

options.text: Its circumference measured end to end
Its length from end to end

questions.explanation: The 280 to 300 millimetre range is the straight-line length of the ball.

questions.stem: What is the minimum circumference of the ball measured end to end?
questions.explanation: Measured around its length, the ball must be between 740 and 770 millimetres.

questions.stem: What is the maximum circumference of the ball measured end to end?
questions.explanation: Measured around its length, the ball must be between 740 and 770 millimetres.

questions.stem: Which measurement of the ball must be between 740 and 770 millimetres?

options.text: Its circumference measured end to end
Its length from end to end

questions.explanation: The 740 to 770 millimetre range is the distance around the ball lengthways, passing over both ends.

questions.stem: A ball's circumference measured end to end is 735 millimetres. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is 5 millimetres under the minimum
It is within the permitted range
It is 5 millimetres over the maximum
It is 35 millimetres under the minimum

questions.explanation: The end-to-end circumference must be at least 740 millimetres, so 735 is 5 millimetres short.

questions.stem: What is the minimum circumference of the ball around its width?
questions.explanation: Measured around the middle, the ball must be between 580 and 620 millimetres.

questions.stem: What is the maximum circumference of the ball around its width?
questions.explanation: Measured around the middle, the ball must be between 580 and 620 millimetres.

questions.stem: Which measurement of the ball must be between 580 and 620 millimetres?

options.text: Its circumference measured end to end
Its height when standing on one end
Its length from end to end

questions.explanation: The 580 to 620 millimetre range is the distance around the ball at its widest point.

questions.stem: A ball's circumference around the middle is 625 millimetres. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is 5 millimetres over the maximum
It is 45 millimetres over the maximum
It is 5 millimetres under the minimum
It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: The circumference around the width can be no more than 620 millimetres, so 625 is 5 millimetres over.

questions.stem: Which of the ball's three size measurements has the largest permitted figures?

options.text: The length from end to end
The circumference measured end to end

questions.explanation: The end-to-end circumference is 740 to 770 millimetres, larger than the width circumference (580 to 620) and the length (280 to 300).

questions.stem: A ball is 290 millimetres long, 775 millimetres around its length and 600 millimetres around its width. Which measurement is outside the law?

options.text: The circumference measured end to end

questions.explanation: The end-to-end circumference may be no more than 770 millimetres. The length and width circumference are both in range.

questions.stem: A ball is 302 millimetres long, 760 millimetres around its length and 610 millimetres around its width. Which measurement is outside the law?

options.text: No measurement: the ball is within the law

questions.explanation: The length may be no more than 300 millimetres. The two circumferences are both in range.

questions.stem: What is the minimum weight of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball must weigh between 410 and 460 grams.

questions.stem: What is the maximum weight of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball must weigh between 410 and 460 grams.

questions.stem: A ball weighs 470 grams. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: The heaviest a ball may be is 460 grams, so 470 is 10 grams over.

questions.stem: A ball weighs 400 grams. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: The lightest a ball may be is 410 grams, so 400 is 10 grams under.

questions.stem: A ball weighs 435 grams. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: Any weight from 410 to 460 grams is acceptable, and 435 falls inside that range.

questions.stem: A ball is 290 millimetres long, 610 millimetres around its width and weighs 465 grams. What is wrong with it?
questions.explanation: The length and width circumference are in range, but the weight limit is 460 grams.

questions.stem: What is the lowest air pressure the ball may have at the start of play, in pounds per square inch?
questions.explanation: At the start of play the ball's pressure must be between 9.5 and 10.0 pounds per square inch.

questions.stem: What is the highest air pressure the ball may have at the start of play, in pounds per square inch?
questions.explanation: At the start of play the ball's pressure must be between 9.5 and 10.0 pounds per square inch.

questions.stem: What is the lowest air pressure the ball may have at the start of play, in kilopascals?
questions.explanation: In kilopascals, the permitted range at the start of play is 65.71 to 68.75.

questions.stem: What is the highest air pressure the ball may have at the start of play, in kilopascals?
questions.explanation: In kilopascals, the permitted range at the start of play is 65.71 to 68.75.

questions.stem: What is the permitted air pressure range at the start of play, in kilograms per square centimetre?
questions.explanation: In kilograms per square centimetre, the ball's pressure must be 0.67 to 0.70 at the start of play.

questions.stem: At what point does the law require the ball's air pressure to be within the stated range?

options.text: When the ball leaves the factory
At the start of each half

questions.explanation: The pressure figures in law apply to the ball at the start of play.

questions.stem: A match ball is checked just before kick-off and reads 11 pounds per square inch. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is within the permitted range
It is 1 pound per square inch over the maximum
It is 1 pound per square inch under the minimum
It is 1.5 pounds per square inch over the maximum

questions.explanation: The most the ball may be inflated to at the start of play is 10.0 pounds per square inch.

questions.stem: A match ball is checked just before kick-off and reads 9 pounds per square inch. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It is 0.5 pounds per square inch over the maximum
It is within the permitted range
It is 1 pound per square inch under the minimum
It is 0.5 pounds per square inch under the minimum

questions.explanation: The least the ball may be inflated to at the start of play is 9.5 pounds per square inch.

questions.stem: A match ball is checked just before kick-off and reads 9.8 pounds per square inch. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It must be changed for a spare ball
It is within the permitted range

questions.explanation: Anything from 9.5 to 10.0 pounds per square inch is acceptable at the start of play.

questions.stem: The law gives the ball's air pressure in three units. Which of these is one of them?
questions.explanation: The law states the pressure in kilopascals, kilograms per square centimetre and pounds per square inch.

questions.stem: What may the ball be made of?

options.text: Any material the match organiser chooses
Leather or a suitable synthetic material

questions.explanation: The ball can be leather or a suitable synthetic material.

questions.stem: May the surface of the ball be treated?

options.text: Yes, but only to make it easier to grip
Yes, but only to make it water resistant
Yes, to make it water resistant and easier to grip
No, the surface must be left untreated

questions.explanation: The ball may be treated both to resist water and to improve grip.

questions.stem: For which two purposes does the law allow the ball to be treated?
questions.explanation: Treatment is allowed to make the ball water resistant and easier to grip.

questions.stem: A match ball is made entirely of synthetic material, with no leather. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: It complies only in wet weather
It complies if the material is suitable
It complies only if both captains agree
It does not comply, because the ball must be leather

questions.explanation: A suitable synthetic material is permitted as an alternative to leather.

questions.stem: In which matches does the law allow smaller balls to be used?
questions.explanation: Smaller balls may be used when the players are young.

questions.stem: The organisers of an under-10 festival want to use a smaller ball than the adult size. What does the law say?

options.text: A smaller ball may be used only in training
Smaller balls may be used for young players
A smaller ball needs World Rugby's approval
The standard dimensions apply at every age

questions.explanation: The law expressly allows smaller balls for matches between young players.

questions.stem: What does the law say about spare balls during a match?

options.text: They may be used only after half-time
At least three must be provided

questions.explanation: The law permits spare balls to be available during a match.

questions.stem: Does the law require a match to have spare balls?

options.text: No, a match is played with a single ball throughout
Yes, at least one spare is required
No, it permits them but does not require them
Yes, one for each touchline is required

questions.explanation: The law says spare balls may be available. It does not make them compulsory.

questions.stem: A ball is 290 millimetres long, 760 millimetres around its length, 610 millimetres around its width and weighs 450 grams. How does it compare with the law?

options.text: Every measurement is within the permitted range
Its width circumference is too large

questions.explanation: Length 280 to 300, end-to-end circumference 740 to 770, width circumference 580 to 620 and weight 410 to 460 are all satisfied.

questions.stem: What is the most players a team may have in the playing area during play?
questions.explanation: Each team may have no more than 15 players in the playing area while play is going on.

questions.stem: Who may authorise a match to be played with fewer than 15 players in each team?
questions.explanation: It is the match organiser who can authorise matches with fewer than 15 players a side.

questions.stem: A team tells the referee that its opponents have 16 players on the field, and they do. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Having too many players on the field is sanctioned with a penalty, and the captain is told to reduce the number.

questions.stem: A team is found to have too many players on the field after its opponents object. What happens to the points already scored?

options.text: The most recent score by that team is cancelled
The referee decides which scores stand
The score stays as it was at the time of the objection
All points scored by that team are cancelled

questions.explanation: The score at the moment the objection is made is left unaltered.

questions.stem: A team has too many players on the field. Whom does the referee order to reduce the number?

options.text: The player who came on last

questions.explanation: The referee tells the captain of the offending team to reduce the number of players.

questions.stem: Who may raise an objection with the referee about the number of players in a team?
questions.explanation: A team may object to the referee about how many players its opponents have.

questions.stem: For an international match, what is the most replacements a union may nominate?
questions.explanation: A union may name up to eight replacements for an international match.

questions.stem: For a match that is not an international, who decides how many replacements may be nominated?
questions.explanation: Below international level the match organiser sets the number of replacements, up to a maximum of eight.

questions.stem: A league is deciding how many replacements its clubs may nominate. What is the highest number it can allow?
questions.explanation: The match organiser decides the number, but it cannot be more than eight.

questions.stem: When may a replacement come on?

options.text: When the ball is dead and the referee gives permission
At any time, provided the referee gives permission
Whenever the ball is dead, with or without permission
Only at a scrum, lineout or restart kick

questions.explanation: Both conditions apply: the ball must be dead and the referee must have given permission.

questions.stem: A replacement runs on without the referee's permission, and the referee believes it was done to gain an advantage. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Joining the match without permission to gain an advantage is misconduct, and the sanction is a penalty.

questions.stem: A player returns from treatment without permission and joins the defensive line, and the referee believes this was to gain an advantage. What is the player guilty of?
questions.explanation: Re-joining without the referee's permission in order to gain an advantage is treated as misconduct.

questions.stem: What do the laws call a player who comes on for a team-mate for tactical reasons?
questions.explanation: The laws use the word replacement for a player who comes on for a team-mate, whether because of injury or for tactical reasons.

questions.stem: A squad has 15 players or fewer. What is the minimum number of front-row players it must contain?
questions.explanation: A squad of 15 or fewer needs at least three front-row players.

questions.stem: A squad has 18 players. What is the minimum number of front-row players it must contain?
questions.explanation: Squads of 16, 17 or 18 need at least four front-row players.

questions.stem: A squad has 20 players. What is the minimum number of front-row players it must contain?
questions.explanation: Squads of 19 to 22 need at least five front-row players.

questions.stem: A squad has 23 players. What is the minimum number of front-row players it must contain?
questions.explanation: A squad of 23 needs at least six front-row players.

questions.stem: A squad of 17 must be able to replace which front-row players at the first time of asking?

options.text: Either a prop or a hooker
A loose-head prop, a tight-head prop and a hooker
Both a prop and a hooker

questions.explanation: Squads of 16 to 18 must be able to replace either a prop or a hooker the first time one is needed.

questions.stem: A squad of 22 must be able to replace which front-row players at the first time of asking?

options.text: Either a prop or a hooker
A loose-head prop, a tight-head prop and a hooker
Both a prop and a hooker

questions.explanation: Squads of 19 to 22 must be able to replace both a prop and a hooker the first time each is needed.

questions.stem: A squad of 23 must be able to replace which front-row players at the first time of asking?

options.text: A loose-head prop, a tight-head prop and a hooker
Two props of either side, but not a hooker
A loose-head prop and a hooker, but not a tight-head
A hooker and one prop, whichever side is needed

questions.explanation: A squad of 23 must be able to cover all three front-row positions the first time each is needed.

questions.stem: Who may amend the minimum number of front-row players in a squad at defined levels of the game?

options.text: The referee, before the match starts
The match organiser, having considered player welfare

questions.explanation: A match organiser may change the front-row minimums and replacement obligations at defined levels, after taking player welfare into account.

questions.stem: Squads are set at 23, but one team can name only two front-row replacements. How many players may that team nominate?
questions.explanation: A team that can provide only two front-row replacements in a 23-player competition is limited to a squad of 22.

questions.stem: Before the match, what must each team tell the appropriate match official about its front row?

options.text: Who can play there, but not in which positions
Only who its three starting front-row players are
Who can play there, including replacements, and in which positions
Only how many front-row players are in its squad

questions.explanation: Teams must identify their front-row players and possible front-row replacements, and say which front-row positions each can play.

questions.stem: A replacement was listed before the match as able to play hooker only. Scrums are contested. Where may this player play in the front row?

options.text: At hooker or at either prop
At any front-row position if the referee agrees
At any front-row position if the captain asks

questions.explanation: In contested scrums a player may play only in the front-row position or positions designated before the match.

questions.stem: A player listed as a front-row replacement is picked to start the match at flanker. Is this allowed?

options.text: Only if the opposing captain agrees
Only if the match organiser gives permission
No, a front-row replacement must start on the bench
Yes, a front-row replacement may start in another position

questions.explanation: The law allows a replacement front-row player to start the match in a different position.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for making sure front-row players and their replacements are suitably trained and experienced?
questions.explanation: It is each team's own responsibility to ensure its front-row players and replacements are suitably trained and experienced.

questions.stem: When may a player who is not a front-row player or front-row replacement play in the front row?

options.text: Only in the second half of the match
Only with the opposing captain's agreement
Only when no front-row replacement is available

questions.explanation: Another player may go into the front row only when the team has no front-row replacement available.

questions.stem: When do scrums become uncontested?

options.text: Whenever either captain asks for it
When either team cannot field a suitably trained front row, or the referee orders it
Only when both teams cannot field a suitably trained front row
Whenever either team is reduced to 14 players

questions.explanation: Scrums go uncontested if one team cannot put out a suitably trained front row, or if the referee orders it.

questions.stem: Who may set the conditions under which a game can start with uncontested scrums?
questions.explanation: The match organiser may stipulate when a game is allowed to begin with uncontested scrums.

questions.stem: Scrums have become uncontested because of an injury. How many players from each team must take part in each scrum?
questions.explanation: Uncontested scrums that result from an injury, yellow card or sending off must still be played with eight players a side.

questions.stem: A prop is sent off and scrums become uncontested as a result. The team has 14 players. How many must it put into each scrum?
questions.explanation: Even a team reduced to 14 must put eight players into an uncontested scrum caused by a sending off.

questions.stem: A front-row player leaves the field injured. When does the referee ask the team whether it can continue with contested scrums?

options.text: At the next stoppage of any kind

questions.explanation: The referee enquires at the next scrum after the front-row player has left.

questions.stem: Scrums are uncontested because a prop is in the sin-bin and no cover was available. The prop returns. What may now happen?

options.text: Scrums stay uncontested for the rest of the match
Scrums stay uncontested until the next score

questions.explanation: If the player returns, or another front-row player comes on, contested scrums can start again.

questions.stem: In a match with squads of 23, a prop goes off injured and the referee has to order uncontested scrums. Can the prop be replaced?

options.text: Yes, but only by another forward
No, the team continues with one player fewer
Yes, by any replacement who has not yet played

questions.explanation: With squads of 23, a player whose departure causes uncontested scrums cannot be replaced.

questions.stem: A prop is shown a yellow card. The players left on the field cannot form a contested front row, but a front-row replacement is on the bench. What does the team do?

options.text: Chooses any player on the field to play prop
Brings on the front-row replacement as an extra player
Plays uncontested scrums until the prop returns
Nominates another player to leave so the front-row replacement can come on

questions.explanation: The team takes off a player of its choice so that the available front-row player can come on and scrums stay contested.

questions.stem: A flanker is nominated to leave the field so that a replacement prop can cover for a yellow-carded prop. When may the flanker return?

options.text: Only at half-time, if the referee agrees
At the next stoppage in play, with permission
When the suspension ends, or to act as a replacement
Not at all for the rest of that match

questions.explanation: The nominated player stays off until the yellow-card period is over, unless coming back on as a replacement.

questions.stem: A hooker is sent off. To keep scrums contested, the team takes off a wing so a replacement hooker can come on. What is the wing's status?

options.text: The wing may be used later as a replacement
The wing may take no further part in the match
The wing may return after 10 minutes
The wing may return only at half-time

questions.explanation: When a front-row player is sent off, the player nominated to make way may later act as a replacement.

questions.stem: A player is replaced because of injury. May that player return later in the match?

options.text: Yes, but only to replace another injured player
Yes, once the team doctor has cleared the player
Yes, but only in the second half
No, an injured player may not return once replaced

questions.explanation: A player replaced through injury cannot come back on.

questions.stem: At national representative level, a player is treated as injured when which person advises that continuing would be unwise?
questions.explanation: At national representative level it takes the opinion of a doctor. The referee may also decide a player should not continue.

questions.stem: In a club match with no medically trained person present, a player looks too hurt to carry on. On whose agreement may the player be replaced?
questions.explanation: Where nobody medically trained is present, the player may be replaced if the referee agrees.

questions.stem: The referee decides, without any medical advice, that a player should not continue. What happens?

options.text: The referee orders the player to leave the playing area
The referee must wait for a medical opinion
The player's captain makes the final decision
The player may choose to stay on

questions.explanation: The referee can decide, with or without medical advice, that a player should not continue, and orders the player off.

questions.stem: May the referee order an injured player to leave the playing area to be medically examined?

options.text: Only if the player's captain agrees
Yes, the referee has that power
No, only a doctor can require it

questions.explanation: The referee may send an injured player off the playing area for a medical examination.

questions.stem: A player with a blood injury is temporarily replaced. Within how long must the player be available to return before the replacement becomes permanent?
questions.explanation: If the player cannot return within 15 minutes of actual time after leaving, the replacement becomes permanent.

questions.stem: When may a player who left with a blood injury return to play?

options.text: Once at least five minutes have passed
Only at the start of the next half
As soon as the bleeding has been controlled or covered

questions.explanation: The player comes back as soon as the bleeding is controlled, covered, or both.

questions.stem: The time limit for a blood replacement is measured in which kind of time?
questions.explanation: The 15 minutes is actual time, meaning continuous elapsed time, not playing time.

questions.stem: In an international match, who decides whether an injury is a blood injury that needs a temporary replacement?
questions.explanation: In internationals the match-day doctor decides whether a blood injury calls for a temporary replacement.

questions.stem: How do the laws define a blood injury?

options.text: A wound that will need stitches
Any cut that has broken the skin
Any blood visible on a player's kit

questions.explanation: A blood injury means bleeding that is active and not under control.

questions.stem: A player has suspected concussion. What must happen?

options.text: The player is removed immediately and permanently
The player's captain decides whether the player continues
The player leaves for 10 minutes and may then return
The player is checked at the next stoppage and may carry on

questions.explanation: Any player with concussion or suspected concussion must leave the playing area at once and may not return.

questions.stem: What is the process for dealing with concussion or suspected concussion called?
questions.explanation: The immediate, permanent removal of a player with suspected concussion is known as Recognise and Remove.

questions.stem: In a match approved for the head injury assessment process, how long does a player have to return before the temporary replacement becomes permanent?
questions.explanation: For a head injury assessment the limit is 12 minutes of actual time. The 15-minute limit applies to blood injuries.

questions.stem: A player needs a head injury assessment, but the team has already used all its replacements. What happens?

options.text: The player stays on until the next stoppage
The team plays one short during the assessment
The player is still temporarily replaced

questions.explanation: A player going for a head injury assessment is temporarily replaced even if every replacement has already been used.

questions.stem: In a match using the head injury assessment process, when may the game restart after a player leaves for an assessment?

options.text: After a minimum of two minutes
Once the player has been temporarily replaced
As soon as the player has left the field

questions.explanation: Play cannot restart until the temporary replacement for that player is on.

questions.stem: Which matches may use the head injury assessment process?

options.text: Matches approved in advance by World Rugby
Any match where both teams agree
All matches with a doctor present

questions.explanation: The process is available only in matches that World Rugby has approved for it beforehand.

questions.stem: A temporary replacement is cut and bleeding, and the team has used all its replacements. Can the temporary replacement be temporarily replaced?

options.text: Yes, even though all replacements have been used
Only if the original player returns at once
No, the team must play one short
Only if the opposing captain agrees

questions.explanation: A temporary replacement can itself be temporarily replaced, even when all replacements have been used.

questions.stem: A temporary replacement is injured while on the field. What does the law allow?

options.text: The team must play one short
The original player must return at once
The referee must end the temporary replacement
That player may also be replaced

questions.explanation: An injured temporary replacement can be replaced in turn.

questions.stem: A temporary replacement is sent off. Leaving aside the front-row provisions, may the originally replaced player return?

options.text: No, the replaced player may not return
Yes, as soon as medically cleared
Yes, at the start of the next half

questions.explanation: If the temporary replacement is sent off, the original player cannot come back, except to keep scrums contested under the front-row provisions.

questions.stem: A temporary replacement is shown a yellow card. Leaving aside the front-row provisions, when may the originally replaced player return?

options.text: Not at all in that match
Immediately, in place of the suspended player
At the next stoppage in play

questions.explanation: The original player must wait until the yellow-card period has ended, and must still be medically cleared and within the time allowed.

questions.stem: The time allowed for a blood replacement runs out during half-time. What must the replaced player do to stop the replacement becoming permanent?

options.text: Return at the first stoppage of the second half
Report to the referee during half-time
Return to the field immediately at the start of the second half
Return within 15 minutes of the second half starting

questions.explanation: If the time expires during the interval, the player must be back on at the very start of the second half or the replacement is permanent.

questions.stem: A player was replaced for tactical reasons. In which of these situations may that player come back on?

options.text: To replace any player in the last ten minutes
To replace a player who has been shown a yellow card
To replace a player who is tired
To replace a player with a blood injury

questions.explanation: A tactically replaced player may return only in limited cases, one of which is to cover a blood injury.

questions.stem: A flanker replaced for tactical reasons is on the bench. The fly-half then pulls a hamstring, with no foul play involved. May the flanker return in the fly-half's place?

options.text: No, that is not one of the permitted reasons
Yes, if the opposing captain agrees
Yes, any injury allows a return

questions.explanation: An ordinary injury to a player outside the front row does not allow a tactically replaced player to come back on.

questions.stem: A hooker is injured and the only player left who can cover is a prop who was replaced for tactical reasons earlier. May the prop return?

options.text: No, a tactically replaced player cannot return
Only if scrums have already gone uncontested
Only after 20 minutes of playing time
Yes, to replace an injured front-row player

questions.explanation: Replacing an injured front-row player is one of the cases in which a tactically replaced player may return.

questions.stem: A centre is injured by foul play, confirmed by the match officials. May a tactically replaced player come back on in the centre's place?

options.text: Only if the offender was sent off
No, tactically replaced players cannot return
Yes, because the injury was caused by foul play
Only if the centre is a front-row player

questions.explanation: A player who has just been injured through foul play, as verified by the match officials, may be replaced by a tactically replaced player.

questions.stem: Before a tactically replaced player returns to cover a foul-play injury, who must verify that foul play caused the injury?
questions.explanation: It is the match officials who verify that the injury resulted from foul play.

questions.stem: In elite rugby, a tactically replaced player may take the place of a team-mate who received a qualifying red card after how much playing time?
questions.explanation: In elite rugby only, the replacement for a qualifying red card can come on once 20 minutes of playing time have passed.

questions.stem: At which level of the game may a red-carded player be replaced by a team-mate after 20 minutes?
questions.explanation: The 20-minute replacement for a qualifying red card applies only in elite rugby.

questions.stem: Where rolling tactical replacements are in use, what is the most interchanges a team may make?
questions.explanation: The number of interchanges under rolling replacements may not be more than 12.

questions.stem: Who may introduce rolling tactical replacements at defined levels of the game?
questions.explanation: A match organiser may bring in rolling tactical replacements at defined levels within its jurisdiction.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for the administration and rules of rolling replacements?
questions.explanation: The match organiser that introduces rolling replacements is responsible for administering them.

questions.stem: Which World Rugby regulation must all items of players' clothing comply with?
questions.explanation: Everything a player wears has to comply with World Rugby Regulation 12.

questions.stem: Which items make up the basic kit a player wears?

options.text: Jersey, shorts and underwear, socks and boots
Jersey, shorts, boots and shin guards
Jersey, shorts, socks and a mouth guard

questions.explanation: The basic kit is a jersey, shorts and underwear, socks and boots. Mouth guards, shin guards and headgear are optional extras.

questions.stem: How far down the arm must the sleeve of a jersey reach, at the least?

options.text: All the way to the elbow
One third of the way from the shoulder point to the elbow
Half-way from the shoulder point to the elbow

questions.explanation: A jersey sleeve must cover at least half the distance from the point of the shoulder to the elbow.

questions.stem: A player has cut the sleeves off a jersey at the shoulder seam. Does the jersey comply with the law?

options.text: No, the sleeve must reach the elbow
Yes, provided the whole team does the same
No, the sleeve must reach at least half-way to the elbow

questions.explanation: The sleeve has to extend at least half-way from the shoulder point to the elbow.

questions.stem: Under the definitions, where must a pair of shorts end?

options.text: At the top of the calf

questions.explanation: Shorts start at the waist and end above the knees.

questions.stem: Under the definitions, how must a pair of shorts be held up?

options.text: By a belt with a buckle, or by braces
By being stitched or clipped to the jersey
By braces worn over the shoulders
By an elasticated waistband, a draw string, or both

questions.explanation: Shorts have an elasticated waistband, a draw string, or both, and are not attached to the jersey or underwear.

questions.stem: Under the definitions, which garments may a jersey be attached to?

options.text: Neither the shorts nor the underwear
Both the shorts and the underwear

questions.explanation: A jersey is a separate shirt for the upper body. It is not attached to shorts or underwear.

questions.stem: Under the definitions, how long may the legs of a player's underwear be?

options.text: Any length, if worn under shorts
Short or absent, ending above the knees
Down to the ankles, if made of cotton blend
Down to the knees but no lower

questions.explanation: Underwear has short legs or none and ends above the knees. Long tights or leggings are a separate permitted item.

questions.stem: What must permitted supports be made of?

options.text: Rigid plastic with a foam lining

questions.explanation: Supports are allowed if they are washable and made of elasticated or compressible material.

questions.stem: Which of these may a player wear?
questions.explanation: Shin guards are a permitted extra. Gloves, jewellery and shorts with sewn-in padding are not allowed.

questions.stem: Where must ankle supports be worn?

options.text: Either under or over the socks

questions.explanation: Ankle supports are permitted only when worn under the socks.

questions.stem: How high up the leg may an ankle support extend?

options.text: No higher than the top of the sock
No higher than one third of the length of the shin
No higher than half the length of the shin

questions.explanation: An ankle support may not reach higher than a third of the way up the shin.

questions.stem: An ankle support worn under the sock reaches half-way up the shin. Does it comply with the law?

options.text: Yes, provided it is not made of metal
No, ankle supports are not permitted at all
No, it may reach no higher than one third of the way up the shin
Yes, any height below the knee is allowed

questions.explanation: The limit is one third of the length of the shin.

questions.stem: A player wants to wear a rigid ankle support under the sock. What restriction applies to its material?

options.text: It must be covered in foam

questions.explanation: A rigid ankle support is allowed only if it is made of something other than metal.

questions.stem: Which hand covering is a player allowed to wear?
questions.explanation: Fingerless mitts are permitted. Gloves are on the list of items that may not be worn.

questions.stem: Which upper-body protection is on the list of permitted items?

options.text: Foam padding sewn into the jersey
Shoulder pads or approved chest pads

questions.explanation: Shoulder pads and approved chest pads are permitted additional items.

questions.stem: Which of these is listed as a permitted additional item?
questions.explanation: A mouth guard or dental protector is permitted. Watches and chains are jewellery, which may not be worn.

questions.stem: A lock wants to wear headgear. What does the law say?

options.text: Headgear is a permitted additional item
Headgear is permitted only with a doctor's note
Headgear is permitted only for forwards

questions.explanation: Headgear is on the list of permitted additional items for any player.

questions.stem: Which of these may a player use to cover or protect an injury?

options.text: A bandage fastened with safety pins

questions.explanation: Bandages, dressings, thin tape and similar materials are permitted. Rigid items and clips are not.

questions.stem: A player wants to wear goggles. What does the law say?

options.text: Goggles are permitted only in training
Goggles are a permitted additional item
Goggles are permitted only at age-grade level

questions.explanation: Goggles appear on the list of permitted additional items.

questions.stem: What does the law say about studs on the soles of boots?

options.text: Only moulded rubber studs are permitted
Studs of any kind are not permitted
They are permitted, including moulded rubber studs

questions.explanation: Studs on the soles of boots are permitted, and that includes moulded rubber ones.

questions.stem: Long tights or leggings are permitted if they meet certain conditions. What must they be made of?
questions.explanation: Permitted long tights or leggings are cotton blend.

questions.stem: How must the seams of permitted long tights or leggings be arranged?

options.text: With seams on both sides of each leg
With a single outside leg seam
With a single inside leg seam

questions.explanation: Permitted tights or leggings have a single seam on the inside of the leg.

questions.stem: Where must permitted long tights or leggings be worn?
questions.explanation: Long tights or leggings go under the shorts and socks.

questions.stem: A player wishes to wear a headscarf. On what condition is it permitted?

options.text: That it is worn under headgear
That it causes no danger to any player
That it matches the team's colours

questions.explanation: Headscarves and head coverings are permitted provided they are not a danger to the wearer or anyone else.

questions.stem: A team fits its players with devices that record how far and how fast they run. What does the law say?

options.text: They are banned as communication devices
They are permitted only in training
They are permitted only for replacements

questions.explanation: Player monitoring devices are a permitted item. Communication devices are what the law bans.

questions.stem: Which of these is on the list of permitted additional items?
questions.explanation: Goggles are permitted. Gloves, jewellery and padded leggings are all on the banned list.

questions.stem: A player's jersey is stained with blood from a team-mate's cut. May the player keep wearing it?

options.text: Yes, once the stain is dry
No, a blood-contaminated item may not be worn
Yes, if the blood is not the player's own

questions.explanation: No item contaminated by blood may be worn, whoever the blood came from.

questions.stem: What does the law say about wearing a sharp or abrasive item?

options.text: It may be worn by forwards only
It may be worn below the waist only
It may be worn in dry conditions only

questions.explanation: Sharp or abrasive items are on the list of things a player may not wear.

questions.stem: Which of these features makes an item illegal unless the law specifically permits it?
questions.explanation: Items with zippers, buckles, clips, rings, hinges, screws or bolts may not be worn unless the law allows them elsewhere.

questions.stem: A player's knee support has a metal hinge. May it be worn?

options.text: No, items containing hinges may not be worn
Yes, if it is worn under leggings
Yes, if the opposing captain agrees
Yes, if a doctor has prescribed it

questions.explanation: Hinges are among the features that make an item illegal.

questions.stem: Which of these may a player not wear?
questions.explanation: Jewellery is banned. Shin guards, mouth guards and thin tape are all permitted.

questions.stem: A wing comes out for a cold match wearing full-fingered gloves. Are they allowed?

options.text: Yes, but only in cold weather
No, gloves may not be worn
Yes, if the referee is told before kick-off

questions.explanation: Gloves are banned. Only fingerless mitts are permitted.

questions.stem: Which of these is on the list of items a player may not wear?
questions.explanation: Gloves are banned, whereas mitts, goggles and headgear are all permitted additional items.

questions.stem: A player's shorts have padding sewn into them. May they be worn?

options.text: No, shorts with sewn-in padding may not be worn
Yes, if the padding is soft foam
Yes, if the padding is thin

questions.explanation: Shorts or leggings with padding sewn into them are on the banned list.

questions.stem: Which of these leg coverings is on the list of items a player may not wear?

options.text: Cotton blend leggings with a single inside leg seam

questions.explanation: Padded leggings are banned. The other three are permitted additional items.

questions.stem: A player's shoulder pads are of a permitted type, but the referee believes this pair is liable to cause injury. May they be worn?

options.text: No, the referee's opinion means they may not be worn
Yes, a permitted item cannot be refused
Yes, unless the opposing captain objects
Yes, until someone is actually hurt

questions.explanation: An item that is normally permitted may not be worn if the referee thinks it is liable to cause injury.

questions.stem: A scrum-half is found wearing an earpiece that lets the coach speak to the player during play. What does the law say?

options.text: Earpieces are permitted in international matches
Communication devices may not be worn
Earpieces are permitted if the referee can hear them too

questions.explanation: Communication devices are on the list of items a player may not wear.

questions.stem: When may the referee decide that part of a player's clothing is dangerous or illegal?

options.text: Only before the match or at half-time

questions.explanation: The referee can make that decision at any point.

questions.stem: During the match the referee decides that a player's boot studs are dangerous. What must the referee do?

options.text: Award a penalty to the opposition
Order the player to remove the item
Show the player a yellow card

questions.explanation: When the referee decides an item is dangerous or illegal, the player must be ordered to remove it.

questions.stem: The referee has ordered a player to remove a dangerous item. When may the player take part in the match again?

options.text: At the next stoppage, whatever the player is wearing
When the item has been removed or made harmless

questions.explanation: The player stays out of the match until the item is removed or rendered harmless.

questions.stem: Before the match an assistant referee tells a player that a banned item must come off. The player is later found wearing it on the playing area. What happens to the player?

options.text: The player is sent off for misconduct
The player is told again to remove it
The player is shown a yellow card

questions.explanation: A player who was warned at the pre-match inspection and is then found wearing the banned item on the playing area is sent off.

questions.stem: A player warned at the pre-match inspection is found wearing the banned item during play and is sent off. How does play restart?

options.text: With a scrum to the team last in possession
With a free-kick to the opposition
With a penalty to the opposition
With a scrum to the opposition

questions.explanation: The sanction that goes with this sending off is a penalty.

questions.stem: A player asks to leave the playing area to change a muddy jersey. What must the referee do?

options.text: Allow it at the next stoppage
Allow it once in each half
Refuse, because the jersey is not bloodstained
Allow it if the opposing captain agrees

questions.explanation: Players may leave the playing area to change clothing only when it is bloodstained.

questions.stem: In which circumstance may the referee let a player leave the playing area to change an item of clothing?

options.text: When the item is the wrong colour
When the item is soaked through

questions.explanation: Bloodstained clothing is the only reason for which a player may leave the playing area to change.

questions.stem: What is the longest a match may last, not counting time lost or extra-time?
questions.explanation: A match lasts no more than 80 minutes, plus time lost.

questions.stem: What is the longest each half may last, before time lost is added?
questions.explanation: Each half is no more than 40 minutes, plus time lost.

questions.stem: In which situation may a match go beyond 80 minutes plus time lost?

options.text: Whenever the scores are level at full time
When both captains ask to play on
When extra-time has been authorised for a drawn knock-out match
When the referee judges the match too close to end

questions.explanation: Extra-time is played only where the match organiser has authorised it for a drawn match in a knock-out competition.

questions.stem: Who may authorise extra-time for a drawn match in a knock-out competition?
questions.explanation: Extra-time has to be authorised by the match organiser.

questions.stem: A knock-out match is drawn after 80 minutes and the match organiser has made no provision for extra-time. May the referee order extra-time?

options.text: No, extra-time must be authorised by the match organiser
Yes, but only ten minutes each way
Yes, the referee may order it in any drawn match

questions.explanation: Without the match organiser's authorisation the match does not go beyond 80 minutes plus time lost.

questions.stem: What is the longest the half-time interval may last?
questions.explanation: Half-time is an interval of no more than 15 minutes.

questions.stem: Who decides how long half-time lasts, up to the maximum?
questions.explanation: The match organiser sets the length of the interval, which may not exceed 15 minutes.

questions.stem: During half-time, who may leave the playing enclosure?

options.text: Nobody: all must stay in the playing enclosure
The teams and the match officials

questions.explanation: Both the teams and the match officials are allowed to leave the playing enclosure during the interval.

questions.stem: For which matches may the match organiser reduce the length of a match?
questions.explanation: The power to shorten a match applies to non-international matches.

questions.stem: In a non-international match, who has the first say on reducing the length of the match?
questions.explanation: The match organiser may decide to reduce the length. Only if it does not decide do the teams, and then the referee, come into it.

questions.stem: The match organiser has not set the length of a non-international match. Who decides it next?
questions.explanation: If the match organiser has not decided, the two teams agree the length between them.

questions.stem: The match organiser has not set the match length and the two teams cannot agree. Who decides?
questions.explanation: When the teams cannot agree on the length of the match, the referee decides.

questions.stem: Who keeps the time in a match?
questions.explanation: The referee keeps the time, although the duty can be delegated.

questions.stem: To whom may the referee delegate time-keeping?

options.text: An official time-keeper and nobody else
The assistant referees and nobody else
The assistant referees, an official time-keeper, or both

questions.explanation: Time-keeping can be handed to either or both assistant referees, to an official time-keeper, or to a combination.

questions.stem: When time-keeping has been delegated, what must the referee do at each stoppage?

options.text: Tell both captains how much time was lost
Note the stoppage and report it after the match
Signal the stoppage to whoever is keeping time
Stop a personal watch and say nothing

questions.explanation: The referee signals every stoppage to those keeping the time.

questions.stem: There is no official time-keeper and the referee is unsure of the correct time. Whom does the referee consult first?
questions.explanation: The referee asks one or both assistant referees. Others may be consulted only if the assistant referees cannot help.

questions.stem: There is no official time-keeper, the referee is unsure of the time, and the assistant referees cannot help. What may the referee do?

options.text: Restart the half from the beginning
Add five minutes to be safe

questions.explanation: Only when the assistant referees cannot help may the referee consult other people about the time.

questions.stem: What do the laws mean by playing time?

options.text: Actual time, excluding time lost for stoppages
The time shown on the stadium clock
The time remaining in the half

questions.explanation: Playing time is actual time with the time lost for stoppages taken out.

questions.stem: What do the laws mean by actual time?

options.text: Time the ball is in open play

questions.explanation: Actual time is simply continuous elapsed time. Playing time is what excludes stoppages.

questions.stem: For how long may the referee normally stop play for an injured player?
questions.explanation: The referee may stop play for an injury for up to one minute.

questions.stem: A player is seriously injured and cannot be moved within a minute. What may the referee do?

options.text: Restart play around the injured player
Restart play after one minute regardless
Allow more than one minute for the player to be removed

questions.explanation: For a serious injury the referee has discretion to allow more than a minute for the player to be taken from the playing area.

questions.stem: Apart from injury, for what else may the referee stop play and allow time?

options.text: A team talk requested by a captain

questions.explanation: The referee may stop play to consult the other officials.

questions.stem: Once the ball is dead, for which of these may the referee allow time?

options.text: A drinks break at each scrum

questions.explanation: Once the ball is dead, time may be allowed for replacements, replacing or repairing clothing, re-tying a boot-lace and retrieving the ball.

questions.stem: When may the referee allow time for a replacement to be made?

options.text: Once the ball is already dead
At any moment, including during play

questions.explanation: Time for replacing players is allowed only when the ball is already dead.

questions.stem: A player's jersey is ripped. When may the referee allow time for it to be replaced or repaired?

options.text: Once the ball is already dead

questions.explanation: Time for replacing or repairing clothing may be allowed once the ball is already dead.

questions.stem: The ball has gone into the crowd and is dead. What may the referee do about the time needed to get it back?

options.text: Add the time only if there is no spare ball
Allow time for retrieving the ball
Add the time only in the last five minutes of a half

questions.explanation: Retrieving the ball is one of the things for which the referee may allow time once the ball is dead.

questions.stem: Time has expired while play is going on. When does the half end?

options.text: When the next ruck or maul forms
At the exact moment time expires
When the ball next becomes dead, unless an exception applies
When the team in possession loses the ball

questions.explanation: A half ends when the ball becomes dead after time has expired, subject to a few exceptions.

questions.stem: A scrum is awarded just before time expires, and time runs out before it has taken place. What happens?

options.text: The scrum takes place and play continues until the ball is next dead
The half ends as soon as the ball is thrown in
The half ends without the scrum
The scrum takes place only if it is inside a 22

questions.explanation: A scrum, lineout or restart kick awarded before time expired must be completed, with the ball returning to open play.

questions.stem: A lineout awarded before time expired is thrown in after time, and the throw is not straight. Does the half end?

options.text: Yes, unless the other team asks to play on
No, but only one more phase is allowed
Yes, because the ball became dead after time
No, because the lineout was not completed correctly

questions.explanation: The half does not end when a scrum, lineout or restart kick awarded before time is taken incorrectly.

questions.stem: Time has expired and the referee awards a penalty. Does the half end?

options.text: Yes, unless the penalty is within kicking range
No, but the team must kick at goal

questions.explanation: The half does not end when the referee awards a penalty or free-kick.

questions.stem: Time has expired and the referee awards a free-kick. Does the half end?

options.text: Yes, because only a penalty extends the half
No, but only if the free-kick is for a mark

questions.explanation: An award of a free-kick, like a penalty, means the half continues.

questions.stem: After time has expired, a team kicks a penalty straight into touch without tapping it first. What happens?

options.text: The half ends when the ball crosses the touchline
The half ends unless the kick was from inside the 22
The half continues with the lineout

questions.explanation: A penalty kicked into touch without being tapped, and without touching another player, does not end the half.

questions.stem: After time has expired, a player taps a penalty and then kicks the ball into touch. Does the half end?

options.text: No, unless the ball bounced first
No, a lineout follows any penalty kicked to touch
Yes, because the ball was tapped before it went into touch
Yes, but only if the kick was from inside the 22

questions.explanation: The exception covers only a penalty kicked to touch without first being tapped. Once tapped, the ball going dead ends the half.

questions.stem: A try is scored after time has expired. What does the referee allow before ending the half?

options.text: Nothing: the half ends with the try
Time for the conversion to be taken
A scrum to the defending team

questions.explanation: When a try is scored the referee allows time for the conversion.

questions.stem: Must a team attempt the conversion after scoring a try?

options.text: No, it may attempt the conversion or decline it
No, but declining needs the referee's permission
Yes, every try must be followed by an attempt

questions.explanation: The scoring team may choose to take the conversion or to decline it.

questions.stem: Who must tell the referee that a team is declining a conversion?
questions.explanation: The decision to decline is relayed to the referee by the player who scored the try.

questions.stem: What does the try scorer say to the referee to decline a conversion?
questions.explanation: The try scorer tells the referee "no kick".

questions.stem: When must the decision to decline a conversion be relayed to the referee?

options.text: At the end of the half

questions.explanation: The try scorer says "no kick" once the try has been awarded.

questions.stem: A try is scored with seconds left, and the conversion is taken before time elapses. What follows?

options.text: A scrum on the half-way line

questions.explanation: If the conversion is attempted or declined before time runs out, the referee awards a restart kick.

questions.stem: A try is scored with seconds left, and the try scorer declines the conversion before time elapses. What does the referee award?

options.text: A free-kick on the half-way line

questions.explanation: Declining the conversion before time elapses means play goes on with a restart kick.

questions.stem: When a conversion is attempted, from what moment is the time taken?

options.text: From the strike on the ball
From when the ball is placed on the tee
From the referee's whistle after the kick
From when the ball passes the posts

questions.explanation: Time is taken from the moment the kicker strikes the ball.

questions.stem: In which conditions may the referee allow a water break?
questions.explanation: A water break is at the referee's discretion when it is exceptionally hot, humid, or both.

questions.stem: How long is a water break?
questions.explanation: The water break lasts two minutes.

questions.stem: At what point in a half should a water break be taken?

options.text: Whenever a player asks for one

questions.explanation: The break should come around the middle of the half.

questions.stem: A water break should be taken midway through the half at one of two kinds of moment. Which pair is correct?

options.text: After a penalty, or after a free-kick
When the ball is in touch, or after a knock forward
At a scrum, or at a lineout
After a score, or when the ball is dead near the half-way line

questions.explanation: The break should be taken after a score or when the ball is dead near half-way.

questions.stem: Who decides whether a water break is allowed in very hot conditions?
questions.explanation: Allowing a water break is at the referee's discretion.

questions.stem: The referee believes it would be unsafe to continue the match. What may the referee do?

options.text: Suspend it, but only at half-time
End it, but only with both captains' agreement
Nothing until the match organiser has been consulted
End or suspend the match at any time

questions.explanation: The referee has the power to end or suspend a match at any time on safety grounds.

questions.stem: Which match officials have control of every match?

options.text: The referee and the two captains
The referee and two touch judges or assistant referees
The referee, the match doctor and the coaches

questions.explanation: Every match is under the control of the referee and two touch judges or assistant referees.

questions.stem: Who normally appoints the referee?
questions.explanation: The referee is appointed by the match organiser.

questions.stem: No referee has been appointed for a match. What happens first?

options.text: The visiting team appoints a referee
The two teams agree on a referee
The home team appoints a referee

questions.explanation: If nobody has been appointed, the two teams first try to agree on a referee.

questions.stem: No referee has been appointed and the two teams cannot agree on one. Who appoints the referee?
questions.explanation: When the teams cannot agree, the home team appoints the referee.

questions.stem: The referee is injured and cannot finish the match. How is the replacement chosen in the first instance?

options.text: According to the match organiser's instructions
By the choice of the home team's captain
By a vote of the assistant referees
By agreement between the two coaches

questions.explanation: A replacement referee is appointed in line with the match organiser's instructions, if there are any.

questions.stem: The referee cannot finish the match and the match organiser has given no instructions. Who appoints the replacement?
questions.explanation: With no instructions from the match organiser, the referee appoints the replacement.

questions.stem: The referee cannot continue, the match organiser has given no instructions, and the referee is unable to appoint a replacement. Who does?
questions.explanation: As a last resort the home team appoints the replacement referee.

questions.stem: Who organises the toss before the match?
questions.explanation: The referee organises the toss.

questions.stem: At the toss, who tosses the coin and who calls?

options.text: The home captain both tosses and calls
The referee tosses and the home captain calls
The referee tosses and the visiting captain calls
One captain tosses and the other captain calls

questions.explanation: One captain tosses the coin and the other makes the call.

questions.stem: What may the winner of the toss decide?

options.text: Both to kick off and to choose an end
Either to kick off or to choose an end

questions.explanation: The winner picks one of the two: kicking off, or choosing an end.

questions.stem: The captain who wins the toss decides to choose an end. What follows?

options.text: The opponents decide who kicks off
The referee decides who kicks off
The toss winner also kicks off

questions.explanation: If the toss winner chooses an end, the other team has to kick off.

questions.stem: The captain who wins the toss decides to kick off. What follows?

options.text: The toss winner also chooses an end
The ends are decided by a second toss

questions.explanation: If the toss winner takes the kick-off, the other team gets the choice of ends.

questions.stem: Before the match, what must the match officials inspect to see that it conforms with the clothing law?
questions.explanation: The match officials inspect the players' clothing and studs before the match.

questions.stem: During a match, who is the sole judge of fact and of law?

options.text: The referee and assistant referees together

questions.explanation: Within the playing enclosure the referee is the sole judge of fact and of law.

questions.stem: Who keeps the score during a match?
questions.explanation: Keeping the score is one of the referee's duties.

questions.stem: If the match organiser appoints a time-keeper, what does the time-keeper signify?

options.text: The start of each half only

questions.explanation: An appointed time-keeper signifies the end of each half.

questions.stem: When does the referee permit players and replacements to enter the playing area?

options.text: Only at a scrum or lineout
When it is safe to do so

questions.explanation: The referee allows players and replacements on when it is safe.

questions.stem: A player wants to leave the playing area during the match. In general, whose permission is needed?
questions.explanation: Players need the referee's permission to leave the playing area.

questions.stem: From where may a player get water without needing the referee's permission?

options.text: Anywhere in touch during a lineout

questions.explanation: A player may take water from the team's technical area, or from behind the dead-ball line after a try, without asking.

questions.stem: After a try has been awarded, where may a player go for water without the referee's permission, besides the technical area?
questions.explanation: After a try, players may take water from behind the dead-ball line without needing permission.

questions.stem: After the match, to whom does the referee communicate the score?

options.text: The teams and the match organiser

questions.explanation: The referee tells both the teams and the match organiser the score.

questions.stem: A player was sent off. What must the referee give the match organiser?

options.text: Nothing at all, unless the player lodges an appeal
A verbal report on the foul play, within seven days
A written report on the foul play, as soon as possible
