A copy of the match recording, within 48 hours

questions.explanation: After a sending off the referee provides a written report to the match organiser as soon as possible.

questions.stem: For which of these does the referee blow the whistle?

options.text: The beginning and end of each half

questions.explanation: The whistle marks the start and the end of each half, among other things.

questions.stem: When does the referee have the power to stop play by blowing the whistle?

options.text: Only when the ball is dead

questions.explanation: The referee can stop play at any time.

questions.stem: The referee sends off a player and awards a penalty. How is the whistle used?

options.text: Once only, to cover the sending off and the penalty
Once for the sending off and again when the penalty is awarded
Three times in quick succession, then the card
Once, when the penalty is awarded, and not before

questions.explanation: The whistle is blown to caution or send off the offender, and a second time when the penalty or penalty try is awarded.

questions.stem: The referee blows the whistle when the ball becomes dead, with one exception. Which is it?

options.text: When the ball goes into touch
When the ball crosses the dead-ball line
When the ball hits something above the playing area

questions.explanation: The whistle is blown whenever the ball becomes dead, other than after a conversion kick that misses.

questions.stem: The ball becomes unplayable. What does the referee do?

options.text: Waits silently for the ball to emerge

questions.explanation: The referee blows the whistle when the ball becomes unplayable.

questions.stem: The referee suspects that a player on the ground is seriously injured while play continues nearby. What should the referee do?

options.text: Wait for the next scrum or lineout
Blow the whistle to stop play
Let play continue until the ball is dead
Signal to the assistant referee and play on

questions.explanation: The whistle is blown when it would be dangerous to continue or when a serious injury is suspected.

questions.stem: Which of these makes the ball dead?
questions.explanation: The ball is dead when it is in touch or touch-in-goal.

questions.stem: A defender grounds the ball in in-goal. What is the status of the ball?

options.text: It is dead only if an attacker was close by
It is in play until a second player touches it

questions.explanation: The ball is dead once it has been grounded in in-goal.

questions.stem: When is the ball dead in connection with a conversion?

options.text: Once the conversion has been attempted
Only if the conversion is successful
Not until the restart kick is taken

questions.explanation: The ball is dead once a conversion has been attempted, whatever the result.

questions.stem: A dropped goal is scored. What is the status of the ball?

options.text: It is in play if a defender catches it
It is dead only if it then crosses the dead-ball line
It is in play until it lands

questions.explanation: The ball is dead when a try, penalty goal or dropped goal has been scored.

questions.stem: A ball-carrier in in-goal steps on the dead-ball line. What is the status of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball is dead when it or the ball-carrier touches the dead-ball line or anything beyond it.

questions.stem: A high kick strikes a cable hanging above the playing area. What is the status of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball is dead if it hits anything above the playing area.

questions.stem: In the field of play the ball strikes the referee and neither team gains an advantage. What happens?

options.text: A scrum to the team that last played the ball
A free-kick to the team in possession
A scrum to the team going forward

questions.explanation: If nobody gains an advantage from the ball touching the referee, play simply carries on.

questions.stem: In the field of play the ball-carrier runs into the referee and that team gains an advantage from it. What does the referee award?

options.text: A scrum to the team that last played the ball

questions.explanation: When a team gains an advantage in the field of play from contact with the referee, a scrum goes to the team that last played the ball.

questions.stem: A pass hits the referee in midfield and bounces kindly for the opposition, who gain an advantage. Who throws in at the resulting scrum?

options.text: The team in whose half the scrum takes place
The team that last played the ball
The team that did not last play the ball
The team that gained the advantage

questions.explanation: The scrum is awarded to the team that last played the ball, whichever side gained the advantage.

questions.stem: An attacking ball-carrier in in-goal collides with the referee and gains an advantage from the contact. What does the referee award?

options.text: A try where the contact took place
A drop-out to the defending team
A 5-metre scrum to the attacking team

questions.explanation: With the ball in an attacker's possession, the referee awards a try at the place of the contact.

questions.stem: A defender carrying the ball in in-goal collides with the referee and gains an advantage from the contact. What does the referee award?

options.text: A 5-metre scrum to the attacking team
A penalty to the attacking team
A try to the attacking team
A touch down where the contact took place

questions.explanation: With the ball in a defender's possession, the referee awards a touch down at the place of the contact.

questions.stem: In in-goal a loose ball strikes a ball person before anyone can ground it. How does the referee decide what to award?

options.text: By judging what would have happened next
By awarding a touch down in every case
By awarding a try in every case

questions.explanation: The referee judges what would have happened and awards a try or a touch down at the place of the contact.

questions.stem: Which of these are touch judges responsible for signalling?

options.text: Offside at the lineout, scrum, ruck and maul
Obstruction and offside in open play
Knock forwards and throws forward in open play
Touch, touch-in-goal and the result of kicks at goal

questions.explanation: Touch judges and assistant referees signal touch, touch-in-goal and whether kicks at goal succeed.

questions.stem: About which matters may the referee consult the assistant referees?

options.text: Touch and kicks at goal only
Their duties, the law on foul play, and timekeeping
Any matter, but only at half-time

questions.explanation: The referee may consult them on their own duties, on foul play and on timekeeping, and may ask for help with other aspects too.

questions.stem: The referee gives a decision and then sees that the assistant referee had raised the flag for touch. May the referee change the decision?

options.text: Only if the assistant referee insists
Yes, the referee may alter the decision
No, the first decision must stand

questions.explanation: The referee may alter a decision after a flag has been raised for touch, touch-in-goal or foul play.

questions.stem: How many assistant referees or touch judges are there for every match?
questions.explanation: Every match has two assistant referees or two touch judges.

questions.stem: The match organiser has not appointed any assistant referees or touch judges. Who provides them?

options.text: The match is played without any
Each team provides one touch judge

questions.explanation: Unless they are appointed under the match organiser's authority, each team supplies a touch judge.

questions.stem: What is the person nominated to replace an assistant referee or touch judge called?

options.text: The match commissioner or the citing officer
The sideline manager or the match manager
The reserve assistant referee or reserve touch judge
The official time-keeper or the statistician

questions.explanation: The nominated stand-in is the reserve touch judge or reserve assistant referee.

questions.stem: Where is the reserve assistant referee situated during the match?
questions.explanation: The reserve touch judge or reserve assistant referee is positioned in the perimeter area.

questions.stem: May the referee overrule the decision of an assistant referee or touch judge?

options.text: Only with the agreement of both captains
Yes, the referee controls them and may overrule them
No, their flag decisions are final

questions.explanation: The referee has control over the assistant referees and touch judges and may overrule their decisions.

questions.stem: A touch judge is performing unsatisfactorily. What may the referee do?

options.text: Ask for the touch judge to be replaced
Award a penalty against the touch judge's team

questions.explanation: If a touch judge is unsatisfactory the referee may ask for a replacement.

questions.stem: The referee believes a touch judge is guilty of misconduct. What power does the referee have?

options.text: Only to report the matter after the match
None: touch judges answer only to their own club
Only to ask the touch judge to behave
To send the touch judge off and report to the match organiser

questions.explanation: The referee can send off a touch judge for misconduct and report it to the match organiser.

questions.stem: Apart from when judging kicks at goal, where does an assistant referee or touch judge remain?
questions.explanation: There is one on each side of the ground, and each stays in touch except when judging a kick at goal.

questions.stem: Where does an assistant referee or touch judge stand to judge a kick at goal?

options.text: In in-goal, behind the goal posts
On the try line at the corner flag
On the touchline, level with the kicker

questions.explanation: For kicks at goal they stand in in-goal behind the posts, one at or behind each post.

questions.stem: How do the assistant referees or touch judges signal that a kick at goal is successful?

options.text: By pointing to the half-way line

questions.explanation: If the ball goes over the crossbar and between the posts, they raise their flags.

questions.stem: The ball goes into touch. What is the touch judge's first signal?

options.text: Waving the flag from side to side
Holding the flag out horizontally infield
Pointing the flag at the ground

questions.explanation: When the ball or ball-carrier goes into touch or touch-in-goal, the flag is held up.

questions.stem: After raising the flag for touch, where does the assistant referee stand, and what else is signalled?

options.text: At the place the ball was kicked, pointing to the kicker's team
At the nearest 15-metre line, pointing infield
At the place of the throw, pointing to the team entitled to throw in
At the corner flag, pointing to the defending team

questions.explanation: The assistant referee stands where the throw is to be taken and points to the team that throws in.

questions.stem: At a lineout throw the assistant referee keeps the flag raised instead of lowering it. Which of these would explain it?

options.text: The thrower put part of a foot in the field of play
A jumper was lifted before the throw
The throw travelled more than 15 metres

questions.explanation: The flag stays up if the thrower has any part of either foot in the field of play, or if the wrong team throws in.

questions.stem: At a quick throw the assistant referee keeps the flag up. Which of these would explain it?

options.text: The thrower threw to a team-mate who was standing still
The throw was taken from behind the place the ball went out
A different ball was used from the one that went into touch
The lineout had not yet formed

questions.explanation: The flag stays up at a quick throw if another ball is used, or if the ball has been touched by someone other than the thrower or the player who carried it out.

questions.stem: Who decides whether the ball was thrown in from the correct place?

options.text: The captain of the non-throwing team
The assistant referee on that touchline

questions.explanation: The place of the throw is a matter for the referee, not the assistant referee or touch judge.

questions.stem: Who may give an assistant referee the authority to signal for foul play?
questions.explanation: A match organiser may authorise assistant referees to signal for foul play.

questions.stem: How does an assistant referee signal that foul play has been seen?

options.text: By pointing the flag at the offending player
By holding the flag straight up and shouting to the referee
By holding the flag horizontally, pointing infield at right angles to the touchline
By waving the flag above the head

questions.explanation: The foul play signal is the flag held horizontally, pointing infield at right angles to the touchline.

questions.stem: An assistant referee has signalled foul play but play continues. What does the assistant referee do?

options.text: Leaves the touchline to find the reserve official
Runs on at once to tell the referee
Stops signalling touch until the referee responds
Stays in touch and carries on with other duties

questions.explanation: After signalling foul play the assistant referee stays in touch and keeps doing every other duty until play next stops.

questions.stem: When may an assistant referee enter the playing area to report foul play?

options.text: Immediately, whatever is happening in play
At the next stoppage in play, when the referee allows
Only at half-time or after the final whistle
Only when a player has been injured by it

questions.explanation: The assistant referee comes on to report only at the next stoppage and only when the referee allows it.

questions.stem: An assistant referee's verbal report leads to a player being sent off. What must the assistant referee do afterwards?

options.text: Give the referee a written report as soon as possible after the match
Send a written report directly to the player's club
Give evidence only if the player appeals
Nothing more: the verbal report is enough

questions.explanation: The assistant referee submits a written report to the referee, who passes it to the match organiser.

questions.stem: Who may appoint a television match official?
questions.explanation: A television match official is appointed by the match organiser.

questions.stem: Which of these may a television match official be used to clarify?

options.text: Whether the ball was grounded in in-goal
Whether a water break is needed
Whether a team has used all its replacements
Whether the half-time interval ran too long

questions.explanation: The grounding of the ball in in-goal is one of the situations a television match official can clarify.

questions.stem: The assistant referees are unsure whether a penalty kick passed inside the post. May the television match official be used?

options.text: No, kicks at goal are for the assistant referees alone
Yes, where there is doubt whether a kick at goal succeeded
Only in the last ten minutes of a half
Only for conversions, not for penalty kicks

questions.explanation: Doubt about whether a kick at goal was successful is one of the listed uses.

questions.stem: May the television match official be used for foul play?

options.text: Only when a player has been injured

questions.explanation: Foul play, including the sanction, is one of the matters a television match official can clarify.

questions.stem: Who may recommend a review by the television match official?

options.text: The referee and the two head coaches
The two captains, through the referee
The referee, but no other match official
Any match official, including the television match official

questions.explanation: Any match official, the television match official included, can recommend a review.

questions.stem: A non-playing member of a team fails to adhere to the laws. What may happen?

options.text: Nothing: the laws apply only to players
The person may be cautioned or sent off
Only the team's captain can be penalised

questions.explanation: Any additional person who does not follow the laws may be cautioned or sent off, and misconduct charges may follow.

questions.stem: When may accredited first-aid or pitch-side care persons enter the playing area to attend an injured player?

options.text: Only when the ball is dead
At any time it is safe to do so
Only when the referee stops play
Only at a scrum or lineout

questions.explanation: Trained and accredited care persons may come on to treat a player whenever it is safe.

questions.stem: How many medics may follow play, and where are they positioned?

options.text: Up to two, one on either side of the pitch
Up to four, two on either side
One, on the side of the technical zones
Up to two, both on the same side

questions.explanation: There may be up to two medics following play, one on each side of the pitch.

questions.stem: To whom may a medic carry and give water?

options.text: Only a player the medic is treating
Any player in the medic's team

questions.explanation: Medics may carry and provide water only for a player they are treating.

questions.stem: A medic on the field picks up a ball that is in live play. What is the sanction?

options.text: A penalty where play would restart
A scrum where the medic touched the ball
A free-kick where play would restart

questions.explanation: Medics may not field or touch a live ball. The sanction is a penalty where play would restart.

questions.stem: How many nominated water carriers may enter the playing area at a permitted stoppage?
questions.explanation: Two nominated water carriers may enter, provided they do not interfere with play.

questions.stem: In general, during which stoppages may the nominated water carriers enter?

options.text: Half-time and the breaks before extra time
Every scrum and lineout in their own half
Any stoppage at all, however short it may be
A stoppage for an injury, or when a try has been scored

questions.explanation: Water carriers may come on during a stoppage for an injured player or after a try.

questions.stem: In a match with squads of 23, when may water carriers enter?

options.text: Only when a try is scored

questions.explanation: With squads of 23, water carriers come on only when a try has been scored.

questions.stem: In a match with squads of 23, a try is scored. Where does the scoring side take its water?

options.text: At the place where the try was scored
On or near the 10-metre line in its own half

questions.explanation: The scoring side goes to an area on or near the 10-metre line in its own half.

questions.stem: In a match with squads of 23, a try is scored and water carriers come on. When must they leave?

options.text: When the referee blows for the restart kick
When the kicker places the ball

questions.explanation: The water carriers must be off when the conversion is taken.

questions.stem: A penalty try is awarded. May water carriers enter the field?

options.text: Yes, but only the scoring side's carriers
Yes, but only the non-scoring side's carriers
No, water carriers may not enter at a penalty try
Yes, both teams' carriers may enter

questions.explanation: No water carriers may come on when a penalty try is awarded.

questions.stem: Which of these people may not act as a water carrier?
questions.explanation: A water carrier must not be a head coach or a director of rugby.

questions.stem: A team signals a kick at goal. What may the person who brings on the kicking tee also carry?

options.text: Water bottles for the whole team
A towel and water for the forwards
One water bottle, for the kicker only

questions.explanation: The person may carry only the kicking tee and one water bottle, which is solely for the kicker.

questions.stem: When may coaches enter the playing area to attend to their teams?

options.text: At any time, if they stay near the touchline

questions.explanation: Coaches may come on to attend to their teams at half-time.

questions.stem: A water carrier standing in the technical area stops a ball that is still in live play. What is the sanction?

options.text: A warning to the team's coach
A penalty where play would restart
A scrum to the non-offending team
A free-kick at the place of the offence

questions.explanation: Additional persons must not field or touch a live ball, even in the technical area. The sanction is a penalty where play would restart.

questions.stem: Which additional persons may speak to the match officials during the match, and about what?

options.text: Medics, about the treatment of their own player
Water carriers, about the time remaining

questions.explanation: Only medics may approach the match officials, and only about treating their own player.

questions.stem: To whom may the management of replacements be delegated?

options.text: The head coach of the home team
Sideline managers appointed by the match organiser
The two team managers, acting together

questions.explanation: Sideline managers appointed by the match organiser may be given the job of managing replacements.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the advantage law?

options.text: To give the team in possession a second chance
To let the referee delay a difficult decision
To give the offending team time to retire
To keep the game flowing after an infringement

questions.explanation: If the non-offending team gains an advantage after an infringement, the referee may let play go on so the game keeps flowing.

questions.stem: Is the referee obliged to play advantage whenever one is possible?

options.text: Yes, except in the last minute of a half
No, the referee may allow play to continue

questions.explanation: The law says the referee may allow play to continue. It is a matter of judgment, not an obligation.

questions.stem: How do the laws define advantage?

options.text: Any possession of the ball after an opposition infringement
A gain of at least five metres after an infringement
A clear and real tactical or territorial benefit after an opposition infringement
A chance to score within two phases of an infringement

questions.explanation: Advantage is a clear and real benefit, tactical or territorial, that arises after the opposition infringes.

questions.stem: Which two kinds of advantage does the law recognise?
questions.explanation: Advantage may be tactical, territorial, or a mixture of both.

questions.stem: What does tactical advantage mean?

options.text: Play has moved towards the offending team's dead-ball line
The non-offending team has kicked the ball into touch
The non-offending team has an extra player
The non-offending team is free to play the ball as it wishes

questions.explanation: Tactical advantage means the non-offending team has the freedom to play the ball as it chooses.

questions.stem: What does territorial advantage mean?

options.text: Play has moved towards the offending team's dead-ball line
Play has moved towards the nearer touchline
Play has stayed in the same place for several phases
The non-offending team is free to play the ball as it wishes

questions.explanation: Territorial advantage means play has moved towards the dead-ball line of the team that offended.

questions.stem: When a team gains territorial advantage, towards which line has play moved?
questions.explanation: Territory is gained when play moves towards the offending team's dead-ball line.

questions.stem: May an advantage be partly tactical and partly territorial?

options.text: Yes, it may be a combination of the two
No, it must be one or the other

questions.explanation: The law allows an advantage to be a combination of tactical and territorial.

questions.stem: How strong must an advantage be before the referee treats it as gained?

options.text: It must gain at least 10 metres
It must lead to a score
It must be clear and real
It must last at least three phases

questions.explanation: An advantage has to be clear and real. A mere opportunity is not enough.

questions.stem: After a knock forward by Red, Blue have the ball but are under immediate pressure, with only a slim chance of using it. Has advantage been gained?

options.text: Yes, if Blue are in Red's half
No, a mere opportunity is not enough
Yes, once Blue have made one pass
Yes, having the ball is enough

questions.explanation: Advantage must be clear and real. Simply having a chance to do something does not count.

questions.stem: Red knock the ball forward. Blue gather it unopposed, with an overlap outside and time to choose what to do. Which kind of advantage is this?

options.text: None until they cross the half-way line

questions.explanation: Blue are free to play the ball as they wish, which is tactical advantage.

questions.stem: Red knock the ball forward at half-way. Blue pick up and run 30 metres into Red's 22 before being tackled. Which kind of advantage have Blue gained?

options.text: None, because a scrum was due
None, because they did not score

questions.explanation: Play has moved a long way towards Red's dead-ball line, which is territorial advantage.

questions.stem: Who judges whether an advantage has been gained?

options.text: The captain of the non-offending team

questions.explanation: It is the referee who deems whether the non-offending team has, or is unlikely to have, an advantage.

questions.stem: Does the law set a fixed time or distance for advantage?

options.text: No, the referee judges when it ends

questions.explanation: The law gives no time or distance. Advantage ends on the referee's judgment or when a further infringement occurs.

questions.stem: The referee decides that the non-offending team has gained an advantage. What happens next?

options.text: A scrum is awarded to the non-offending team
Play stops for the original sanction
The non-offending captain chooses whether to play on

questions.explanation: Once the advantage has been gained it is over, and the referee simply allows play to carry on.

questions.stem: Blue gain a clear advantage after a Red knock forward. Two phases later Blue drop the ball. May the referee go back to Red's knock forward?

options.text: No, the advantage had already been gained
Yes, because Blue did not score
Yes, if play is still in the same half
Yes, if it is within 30 seconds

questions.explanation: Advantage ended when Blue gained it. What happens afterwards is judged on its own.

questions.stem: The referee decides that the non-offending team is unlikely to gain an advantage. What happens?

options.text: The non-offending captain chooses a sanction
Play is stopped and the sanction for the infringement is applied
A scrum is awarded to the offending team
Play continues until the ball is dead

questions.explanation: If no advantage is likely, the referee stops the game and goes back to the infringement.

questions.stem: Red knock the ball forward. Blue gather it but are immediately driven backwards and gain nothing. What does the referee do?

options.text: Lets play continue because Blue have the ball
Awards Red a scrum because Blue failed to use the ball
Stops play and awards Blue the scrum for the knock forward

questions.explanation: No advantage was gained, so the referee returns to the original infringement and its sanction.

questions.stem: Advantage is being played to Blue for a knock forward by Red. Before gaining any advantage, Blue also knock the ball forward. What does the referee award?

options.text: A scrum to Red, for the second infringement
A scrum to whichever team was going forward
A scrum to Blue, for the first infringement

questions.explanation: When the non-offending team infringes before gaining an advantage, the sanction for the first infringement is applied.

questions.stem: Advantage is being played to Blue. Before gaining it, Blue throw the ball forward. Which infringement does the referee sanction?

options.text: Both, with a scrum to the team in whose half play is

questions.explanation: The referee stops the game and applies the sanction for the first infringement.

questions.stem: Advantage is being played to Blue for offside by Red. Before any advantage is gained, a Blue player commits foul play. How does the referee deal with the foul play?

options.text: By applying the appropriate sanction for it
By ignoring it and returning to the offside
By awarding a scrum to Blue
By awarding a scrum to Red

questions.explanation: Where either infringement is foul play, the referee applies the appropriate sanction for that offence.

questions.stem: Advantage is being played to Blue for a Red offence when Red commit a second offence from which no advantage can come. What does the referee do?

options.text: Lets play continue until Blue lose the ball
Stops play and lets Blue's captain choose the sanction
Stops play and applies only the first sanction
Stops play and applies only the second sanction

questions.explanation: After a second infringement with no advantage possible, the non-offending captain chooses the better sanction.

questions.stem: The offending team commits a second infringement during advantage and no advantage can be gained. Who chooses between the sanctions?

options.text: The captain of the offending team
The captain of the non-offending team

questions.explanation: The captain of the non-offending team is allowed to pick the most advantageous sanction.

questions.stem: During advantage to Blue, Red commit a second penalty offence nearer Red's try line, and no advantage is possible. Which sanction may Blue's captain take?

options.text: A penalty mid-way between the two marks
Whichever of the two is most advantageous
Only the one for the second offence
Only the one for the first offence

questions.explanation: The captain of the non-offending team may choose the most advantageous of the sanctions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a situation in which the referee must not play advantage?

options.text: A scrum wheeling through more than 90 degrees
A throw forward in open play
A knock forward in open play

questions.explanation: A scrum wheeled through more than 90 degrees is on the list of situations where the whistle must go at once.

questions.stem: From which of these may advantage not be played?

options.text: A knock forward in open play

questions.explanation: Advantage is not applied when a quick throw, free-kick or penalty is taken incorrectly.

questions.stem: The ball-carrier collides with the referee and the ball-carrier's team gains an advantage from it. What must the referee do?

options.text: Play advantage to the other team
Wait to see whether a try is scored

questions.explanation: Advantage must not be applied when the ball or ball-carrier touches the referee and either side gains an advantage.

questions.stem: A kick strikes the referee and rebounds to the kicker's opponents, who gain an advantage. What does the referee do?

options.text: Allows the opponents to play on
Plays advantage to the kicker's team

questions.explanation: When either side gains an advantage from the ball touching the referee, play is stopped at once.

questions.stem: At a scrum the ball comes straight out of the far end of the tunnel. May the referee play advantage?

options.text: Yes, if the team that threw in picks it up
No, the whistle must be blown immediately
Yes, if the ball stays close to the scrum
Yes, if the other team picks it up

questions.explanation: Advantage is not applied when the ball comes out of either end of the tunnel.

questions.stem: Which of these scrum events means advantage must not be applied?

options.text: The scrum moving forward two metres
The ball being hooked by the team that threw in
The ball arriving at the number eight's feet
The ball coming out of either end of the tunnel

questions.explanation: The ball emerging from either end of the tunnel requires an immediate whistle.

questions.stem: A scrum wheels through more than 90 degrees. May advantage be applied?

options.text: Yes, to the team with the ball
Yes, if the ball is at the back of the scrum
Yes, to the team that did not cause the wheel
No, the referee must blow the whistle immediately

questions.explanation: A scrum wheeled beyond 90 degrees is stopped at once, with no advantage.

questions.stem: Through what angle must a scrum wheel before the referee must stop play without advantage?
questions.explanation: The figure in law is a wheel of more than 90 degrees.

questions.stem: A prop is forced upwards in a scrum so that both feet leave the ground. What must the referee do?

options.text: Play advantage to the prop's team
Wait until the ball is out of the scrum

questions.explanation: When a player in a scrum is lifted or forced up and loses contact with the ground, play is stopped at once.

questions.stem: In a scrum, which of these means advantage must not be applied?

options.text: A player being lifted so as to lose contact with the ground
A flanker's bind being adjusted during the push
A front-row player striking early for the ball
A pack being pushed steadily backwards

questions.explanation: A player lifted or forced upwards off the ground is one of the listed situations.

questions.stem: A penalty is taken incorrectly, but the ball ends up with the opposing team in space. May the referee play advantage?

options.text: No, advantage is not applied when a penalty is taken incorrectly
Yes, if the opposing captain asks
Yes, the opposing team has a tactical advantage
Yes, but only until the next ruck

questions.explanation: An incorrectly taken penalty means the whistle goes immediately.

questions.stem: A quick throw is taken incorrectly and the ball goes to the opposition. May advantage be played?

options.text: Yes, if the throw travelled five metres
Yes, if no lineout had formed
No, the referee must blow the whistle immediately

questions.explanation: Advantage is not applied when a quick throw is taken incorrectly.

questions.stem: Can advantage continue once the ball has been made dead?

options.text: No, advantage cannot be applied once the ball is dead
Yes, if the non-offending team had the ball

questions.explanation: When the ball is made dead the referee must blow the whistle. Advantage cannot carry on.

questions.stem: During advantage to Blue, the ball is kicked over the dead-ball line. What happens to the advantage?

options.text: It carries on from the restart
It cannot continue, because the ball is dead
It carries on if Blue made the kick

questions.explanation: Advantage must not be applied once the ball has been made dead.

questions.stem: Advantage is being played, but it would be dangerous to let play go on. What must the referee do?

options.text: Let the advantage run its course
Warn the players and play on

questions.explanation: When it would be dangerous to continue, advantage is not applied and the whistle goes at once.

questions.stem: Advantage is being played when the referee suspects that a player has been seriously injured. What must the referee do?

options.text: Play on unless a medic signals
Wait until the advantage is over
Stop play only if the injured player's team has the ball

questions.explanation: A suspected serious injury means play is stopped immediately.

questions.stem: In which of these situations must the referee stop play at once instead of playing advantage?

options.text: The offending team wins a turnover
The ball has been made dead
The non-offending team forms a maul

questions.explanation: Advantage is never applied once the ball has been made dead.

questions.stem: Blue are playing advantage. They work the ball 25 metres upfield and still have free use of it. Which kind of advantage is this?

options.text: No advantage, as only a score counts
A combination of tactical and territorial

questions.explanation: Advantage may be tactical, territorial or a combination of the two.

questions.stem: When advantage does not materialise, which sanction does the referee apply?

options.text: The one for the infringement from which advantage was played
A scrum, whatever the original infringement was
The one nearest the offending team's try line
The one the non-offending captain chooses

questions.explanation: The referee stops the game and applies the sanction for the infringement from which advantage was being played.

questions.stem: The ball touches the referee in the field of play and neither side gains an advantage. Must the referee stop play?

options.text: Yes, unless the ball was kicked
Only if the ball then goes into touch
Yes, whenever the ball touches the referee
No, the whistle is needed only if a side gains an advantage

questions.explanation: Advantage must not be applied when the ball touches the referee and an advantage is gained by either side. Without that, play goes on.

questions.stem: Which of these overrides the playing of advantage?

options.text: Danger to players if play continues
The time left in the half

questions.explanation: Advantage must not be applied when it would be dangerous to let play continue.

questions.stem: How sure must the referee be of a serious injury before stopping play instead of playing advantage?

options.text: A team-mate must signal to the referee
The injured player must ask for help
It must be confirmed by a doctor

questions.explanation: The referee must blow the whistle immediately when it is suspected that a player is seriously injured.

questions.stem: How many points does a team score for a try?
questions.explanation: A try is worth five points.

questions.stem: How many points does a successful conversion add?
questions.explanation: A conversion is worth two points.

questions.stem: How many points is a penalty try worth?
questions.explanation: A penalty try is worth seven points, with no conversion attempted.

questions.stem: How many points does a penalty goal score?
questions.explanation: A penalty goal is worth three points.

questions.stem: How many points does a dropped goal score?
questions.explanation: A dropped goal is worth three points.

questions.stem: A team scores a try and converts it. How many points has it added?
questions.explanation: Five for the try and two for the conversion make seven.

questions.stem: A team scores two tries, one of them converted, and a penalty goal. What is its total?
questions.explanation: Two tries are 10 points, the conversion adds 2 and the penalty goal 3, giving 15.

questions.stem: A team's only scores are a penalty try and a dropped goal. What is its total?
questions.explanation: Seven for the penalty try and three for the dropped goal make 10.

questions.stem: Which two methods of scoring are worth the same number of points?

options.text: A try and a penalty try
A penalty goal and a dropped goal
A conversion and a dropped goal
A try and a penalty goal

questions.explanation: A penalty goal and a dropped goal are each worth three points.

questions.stem: What must an attacking player do to score a try in the opponents' in-goal?

options.text: Catch the ball in the air above in-goal
Kick the ball over the dead-ball line
Be first to ground the ball there
Carry the ball across the try line

questions.explanation: A try is scored when an attacking player is first to ground the ball in the opponents' in-goal.

questions.stem: A scrum is pushed back until it reaches the defending team's try line. Can the attacking side score?

options.text: Yes, if an attacking player is first to ground the ball
No, a try cannot come from a scrum
Only once the ball has left the scrum
No, the scrum must be reset five metres out

questions.explanation: A try can be scored when a scrum, ruck or maul reaches the try line and an attacker is first to ground the ball.

questions.stem: A maul is driven up to the try line and an attacking player in it is first to ground the ball. What is the decision?
questions.explanation: When a maul reaches the try line, an attacking player who is first to ground the ball scores a try.

questions.stem: A ball-carrier is tackled a metre short of the try line and slides over in one continuous movement, grounding the ball first. What is the decision?
questions.explanation: Momentum that carries a tackled player along the ground into in-goal in one continuous movement allows a try.

questions.stem: A tackled player's momentum may carry the player into in-goal to score. How must that movement be made?

options.text: By any means, as long as no opponent is holding on
In one continuous movement along the ground
By getting up and diving over
In two movements, provided the ball is held

questions.explanation: The player's momentum must carry them over in a continuous movement along the ground.

questions.stem: A player is tackled near the opponents' try line and at once reaches out and grounds the ball on the line. What is the decision?
questions.explanation: A player tackled near the try line may immediately reach out and ground the ball to score.

questions.stem: A player tackled near the try line may score by reaching out and grounding the ball. When must the player do so?

options.text: Once the tackler has let go
Before an opponent touches the ball

questions.explanation: The reach to ground the ball must be made immediately.

questions.stem: A player standing in touch-in-goal reaches in and presses down on a loose ball lying in the opponents' in-goal. What is the decision?

options.text: No try, because the player was in touch-in-goal
Try, because the player was not holding the ball

questions.explanation: A player in touch or touch-in-goal can score by grounding the ball in in-goal, provided they are not holding it.

questions.stem: A player who is in touch-in-goal can score by grounding the ball in in-goal on one condition. What is it?

options.text: The player is not holding the ball
The ball is moving towards the dead-ball line
No defender is within a metre
The player has one foot in in-goal

questions.explanation: The grounding counts only if the player in touch or touch-in-goal is not holding the ball.

questions.stem: Where is a penalty try awarded?

options.text: Where the try would have been scored
Where the foul play took place
On the 5-metre line opposite the offence

questions.explanation: A penalty try is awarded between the posts, wherever the foul play happened.

questions.stem: When is a penalty try awarded?

options.text: When a defender is offside near the try line
When foul play by the opposition prevents a probable try
When a team concedes three penalties in its own 22
When any penalty is conceded in in-goal

questions.explanation: A penalty try follows foul play that stops a probable try, or stops it being scored in a better position.

questions.stem: How likely must the try have been for a penalty try to be awarded?
questions.explanation: The test is whether a try would probably have been scored.

questions.stem: Foul play by a defender does not stop a try, but forces it to be scored at the corner instead of near the posts, where it probably would have been. What may the referee award?

options.text: The try, with the conversion moved in front of the posts
A penalty to the attacking team at the restart

questions.explanation: A penalty try can be awarded when foul play prevents a try being scored in a more advantageous position.

questions.stem: What must happen to the player whose foul play leads to a penalty try?

options.text: Nothing further: the penalty try is the sanction
The player must be shown a yellow card or sent off

questions.explanation: The offender must be cautioned with a yellow card or sent off.

questions.stem: After a penalty try, what happens about the conversion?

options.text: The scoring team chooses whether to take it
It is taken in line with the place of the foul play
It is taken from in front of the posts

questions.explanation: A penalty try is worth seven points outright and no conversion is taken.

questions.stem: For a goal to be scored, where must the ball pass?

options.text: Between the posts at any height
Under the crossbar and between the goal posts
Over the crossbar and between the goal posts
Over the crossbar, inside or outside the posts

questions.explanation: A goal needs the ball to go over the crossbar and between the posts.

questions.stem: A kick at goal bounces off the ground and then goes over the crossbar between the posts. Is it a goal?

options.text: No, the ball must not touch the ground first
Yes, for a penalty kick but not a conversion
Yes, if it bounced only once
Yes, a bounce makes no difference

questions.explanation: For any goal, the ball must go over without first touching the ground or a team-mate.

questions.stem: A kick at goal glances off a team-mate of the kicker and then passes over the crossbar. Is it a goal?

options.text: Yes, if the touch was accidental
Yes, if the team-mate was behind the kicker
Yes, any ball over the crossbar counts
No, the ball must not touch a team-mate first

questions.explanation: A goal is not scored if the ball touches a team-mate of the kicker before going over.

questions.stem: A kick at goal strikes a goal post and then passes over the crossbar between the posts. Is it a goal?

options.text: No, the ball must not touch a post
Yes, touching a post does not prevent a goal
Only if it struck the inside of the post

questions.explanation: The ball must not first touch a team-mate or the ground. Touching a post or the crossbar on the way over does not matter.

questions.stem: A kick passes directly above the top of one goal post. How does the referee decide?

options.text: It is no goal, because the ball was not between the posts
It is a goal if the ball would have gone between the posts had they been taller
It is a goal in every case

questions.explanation: A ball that goes higher than the posts is a goal if it would have passed between them had they been taller.

questions.stem: A kick crosses the crossbar and is then blown back into the field of play by the wind. Does the score stand?

options.text: No, the ball must land beyond the posts
No, unless it lands in in-goal

questions.explanation: Once the ball has crossed the crossbar the goal counts, even if the wind blows it back.

questions.stem: Which kinds of kick may be used for a conversion?
questions.explanation: A conversion may be either a place-kick or a drop-kick.

questions.stem: From where is a conversion taken?

options.text: From the place where the try scorer crossed the try line
On a line through the place where the try was awarded, parallel to the touchlines
From directly in front of the posts

questions.explanation: The kick is taken in the field of play, anywhere on the line running through the place the try was awarded.

questions.stem: How far back from the try line may the kicker go to take a conversion?

options.text: Exactly on the 22-metre line, in front of the posts
No further than the 10-metre line, on the line through the try
Any distance within the field of play, on the line through the try
No further than the 22-metre line, on the line through the try

questions.explanation: The kicker may choose any point in the field of play on the line through where the try was awarded.

questions.stem: On which of these may the ball be placed for a conversion?

options.text: Sand, sawdust or a kicking tee

questions.explanation: The ball goes directly on the ground or on sand, sawdust or a kicking tee. Nothing else may be used.

questions.stem: Who may help the kicker by holding the ball at a conversion?
questions.explanation: The kicker may be assisted by a placer, a team-mate who holds the ball.

questions.stem: How long does the kicker have to take a conversion?

options.text: 90 seconds from the award of the try
60 seconds of playing time from the award of the try
60 seconds from when the kicking tee arrives
40 seconds from the award of the try

questions.explanation: The conversion must be taken within 60 seconds of playing time from when the try was awarded.

questions.stem: At a conversion the ball rolls off the tee and has to be placed again. Is the kicker given extra time?

options.text: Yes, the 60 seconds starts again from the new placement
No, the 60 seconds still runs from the award of the try
Yes, provided the referee agrees the wind caused it
Yes, an extra 30 seconds is added for each placement

questions.explanation: The time limit applies even if the ball rolls over and has to be placed again.

questions.stem: A conversion is not taken within the time allowed. What is the sanction?

options.text: A scrum to the opposition at the place of the kick
The kick is retaken within 30 seconds

questions.explanation: A conversion that is not taken in time is disallowed.

questions.stem: Where must the kicker's team-mates be when a conversion is kicked?

options.text: Behind the ball, apart from a placer holding it

questions.explanation: The kicker's team stays behind the ball when it is kicked, except for a team-mate holding it.

questions.stem: A team-mate of the kicker feints to make the defenders charge too early at a conversion. What is the sanction?

options.text: A free-kick to the defending team
A penalty to the defending team

questions.explanation: The kicker's team must do nothing to mislead opponents into charging too soon. If they do, the kick is disallowed.

questions.stem: At a conversion the ball falls over before the kicker has begun the approach. What does the referee allow?

options.text: Only a drop-kick from where the ball lies
The kicker to replace the ball

questions.explanation: If the ball falls over before the approach begins, the kicker is allowed to replace it.

questions.stem: While the kicker replaces a ball that fell over before the approach began, where must the opponents be?
questions.explanation: The opponents stay behind their try line while the ball is being replaced.

questions.stem: At a conversion the ball falls over after the kicker has begun the approach. What may the kicker do?

options.text: Stop and replace it on the tee
Kick it as it lies or attempt a dropped goal
Ask for the 60 seconds to start again

questions.explanation: Once the approach has begun, the kicker may kick the fallen ball or try a dropped goal.

questions.stem: At a conversion the ball falls over, rolls away from the line through the try, and the kicker then kicks it over the crossbar. What is the decision?

options.text: The kick is retaken from the line
The conversion counts only if it was drop-kicked

questions.explanation: A goal kicked after the ball has fallen and rolled off the line still counts.

questions.stem: After the kicker has begun the approach to a conversion, the ball falls over and rolls into touch. What is the decision?

options.text: The kicker may bring the ball back and kick it
A lineout to the defending team

questions.explanation: If the ball rolls into touch after the approach has begun, the kick is disallowed.

questions.stem: Where must the defending team wait at a conversion?

options.text: At their try line, without overstepping it

questions.explanation: All the defenders retire to their try line and must not overstep it until the kicker begins the approach.

questions.stem: When may the defenders start to charge a conversion?

options.text: When the ball is placed on the tee
When the referee blows the whistle
When the kicker's foot strikes the ball
When the kicker moves to begin the approach

questions.explanation: The defenders may charge once the kicker moves in any direction to start the approach.

questions.stem: A defender is lifted by a team-mate to try to block a conversion. Is this allowed?

options.text: No, a player charging or jumping must not be physically supported
Yes, but only one lifter may be used
Yes, if the lifter stays behind the try line
Yes, lifting is allowed as at a lineout

questions.explanation: Defenders may charge or jump, but must not be physically supported by other players.

questions.stem: The defending team shouts as the kicker runs up to a conversion, and the kick misses. What happens?

options.text: The two points are awarded automatically
The kicker retakes the conversion and the defenders may not charge
The kicking team is awarded a penalty at half-way

questions.explanation: If the defenders infringe and the kick fails, it is retaken and they are not allowed to charge.

questions.stem: The defending team charges too early at a conversion, but the kick goes over. What is the decision?

options.text: A penalty to the kicking team at the restart

questions.explanation: When the defenders infringe but the kick is successful, the goal stands.

questions.stem: A conversion is being retaken because the defenders infringed. May the kicker switch from a place-kick to a drop-kick?

options.text: Yes, the kicker may change the type of kick
Only if the tee has been taken away
No, the same type of kick must be used

questions.explanation: On a retake the kicker may repeat all the preparations and may change the type of kick.

questions.stem: At a conversion the ball falls over after the kicker has begun the approach. May the defenders keep charging?

options.text: No, they must stop where they are
Only the nearest defender may continue
Yes, they may continue to charge
No, they must return to the try line

questions.explanation: If the ball falls over after the approach has begun, the opponents may carry on charging.

questions.stem: An opponent charging a conversion gets a hand to the ball, but it still goes over the crossbar between the posts. What is the decision?

options.text: A scrum to the defending team

questions.explanation: If the opposition touches the ball and the kick is still successful, the goal stands.

questions.stem: From which award can a penalty goal be scored?

options.text: Any kick awarded by the referee

questions.explanation: A penalty goal can come only from a penalty.

questions.stem: When must a team indicate that it intends to kick at goal from a penalty?

options.text: Before the opposition has retired 10 metres

questions.explanation: The kicking team must make its intention to kick for goal known without delay.

questions.stem: A team tells the referee it will kick at goal, then decides it would rather kick for touch. What does the law require?

options.text: It may tap and run instead
It may change its mind with the referee's permission
It may change its mind before the tee arrives

questions.explanation: Once the intention to kick at goal has been indicated, the team must kick at goal.

questions.stem: Which of these signals an intention to kick at goal, even if nothing is said to the referee?

options.text: The scrum-half standing over the mark
The arrival of the kicking tee
The kicker picking up the ball
The forwards walking towards the touchline

questions.explanation: The arrival of the tee or sand, or a player making a mark on the ground, signals the intention to kick at goal.

questions.stem: At a penalty a player scrapes a mark on the ground with a boot. What has the team signalled?

options.text: Nothing, until the referee is told
An intention to kick for touch
An intention to take a scrum
An intention to kick at goal

questions.explanation: Making a mark on the ground counts as indicating a kick at goal.

questions.stem: Having indicated a kick at goal, a team taps the penalty and runs instead. What is the sanction?

options.text: A penalty is awarded to the opposition
A free-kick is awarded to the opposition
The kick is disallowed and a scrum is awarded

questions.explanation: A team that has indicated a kick at goal must take it. If it does not, the kick is disallowed and a scrum awarded.

questions.stem: How long does a kicker have to take a penalty kick at goal?

options.text: 60 seconds of playing time from when the intention to kick was indicated
60 seconds from when the penalty was awarded
90 seconds from when the tee arrives
40 seconds from when the ball is placed

questions.explanation: The kick must be taken within 60 seconds of playing time from when the team indicated it would kick at goal.

questions.stem: A penalty kick at goal is not taken within the time allowed. What is the sanction?

options.text: A free-kick is awarded to the opposition
The kick is disallowed and play restarts with a drop-out
The kick is retaken within 30 seconds
The kick is disallowed and a scrum is awarded

questions.explanation: Running out of time means the kick is disallowed and a scrum is awarded.

questions.stem: How must the defending team behave while a penalty kick at goal is being taken?

options.text: Stand still with their hands by their sides
Stand with arms raised but without jumping

questions.explanation: The opposing team must stand still with hands by their sides.

questions.stem: From when must the defenders stand still at a penalty kick at goal?

options.text: From when the kicker starts the approach until the ball is kicked
From when the tee arrives until the ball lands
From when the penalty is awarded until the ball is kicked
Only at the moment the ball is struck

questions.explanation: They must be still from the start of the kicker's approach until the ball has been kicked.

questions.stem: At a penalty a player takes a quick drop-kick at goal without having told the referee, and it goes over. What is the decision?

options.text: No goal, because no intention was indicated

questions.explanation: A goal from a drop-kick stands even if the kicker had not indicated an intention to kick at goal.

questions.stem: At a penalty kick at goal the kicker props the ball on something other than the ground, sand, sawdust or a tee. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Only the ground, sand, sawdust or a kicking tee may be used. Anything else is sanctioned with a scrum.

questions.stem: A defender jumps and deliberately knocks down a penalty kick that was heading for the posts. How does the law describe this?

options.text: Playing the ball in the air

questions.explanation: Intentionally touching the ball to stop a penalty goal is illegal touching.

questions.stem: Which of these must a defending player not do during a penalty kick at goal?
questions.explanation: Defending players must not shout during a penalty kick at goal.

questions.stem: Defenders infringe while a penalty kick at goal is being taken, but the kick is successful. What is the decision?

options.text: The goal stands and no further penalty is awarded
The goal stands and a further penalty is awarded at half-way

questions.explanation: If the kick succeeds despite the infringement, the goal stands and there is no further penalty.

questions.stem: Defenders infringe while a penalty kick at goal is being taken, and the kick misses. Where is the new penalty awarded?

options.text: 10 metres in front of the original mark
On the 5-metre line in front of the posts
5 metres in front of the original mark

questions.explanation: If the kick fails, the non-offending team gets a penalty 10 metres in front of the original mark.

questions.stem: How is a dropped goal scored?

options.text: By kicking a goal from a punt in open play
By drop-kicking the ball into in-goal
By kicking a goal from a place-kick in open play
By kicking a goal from a drop-kick in open play

questions.explanation: A dropped goal is a goal kicked from a drop-kick in open play.

questions.stem: A team is awarded a free-kick, taps it, and the same player at once drop-kicks the ball over the crossbar. What is the decision?

options.text: No goal, and the free-kick is retaken
No goal, and a scrum to the opposition

questions.explanation: A team awarded a free-kick cannot score a dropped goal straight away. The kick counts as unsuccessful and play goes on.

questions.stem: After a free-kick, when may the team that was awarded it next score a dropped goal?

options.text: After the ball has travelled at least 10 metres from the mark
As soon as the free-kick has been tapped and the ball has been passed once
After the ball is next dead, or an opponent has played or touched it or tackled the ball-carrier
After the ball has been passed through at least two pairs of hands

questions.explanation: The restriction lasts until the ball next becomes dead or an opponent has played or touched the ball or tackled the ball-carrier.

questions.stem: A team awarded a free-kick opts for a lineout instead, wins the ball, and drop-kicks a goal before any opponent has touched the ball. What is the decision?

options.text: No goal, and the lineout is retaken
No goal, and a penalty to the opposition
Goal, because the lineout replaced the free-kick

questions.explanation: The restriction on dropped goals still applies when the team chooses a lineout in place of the free-kick.

questions.stem: A team takes a free-kick. An opponent tackles the ball-carrier, the ball is recycled, and the fly-half drops a goal. What is the decision?

options.text: No goal, unless the ball had gone dead first
No goal, because the move began with a free-kick
No goal, and a scrum to the opposition

questions.explanation: Once an opponent has tackled the ball-carrier, the team may score a dropped goal again.

questions.stem: What must happen to a player who commits foul play?

options.text: The player's captain decides the punishment
The player is shown a yellow card in every case
The player is cautioned, shown a yellow card or sent off
The player is sent off in every case

questions.explanation: A player guilty of foul play must be cautioned, shown a yellow card or sent off.

questions.stem: Which of these is one of the headings of foul play under the laws?
questions.explanation: Foul play covers obstruction, unfair play, repeated infringements, dangerous play and misconduct.

questions.stem: Two opponents are running side by side for a loose ball. What contact between them is allowed?

options.text: A push in the back with one hand

questions.explanation: Players running for the ball may not charge or push each other, except shoulder to shoulder.

questions.stem: A player chasing a loose ball shoves an opponent in the back with both hands to get there first. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Only shoulder-to-shoulder contact is allowed when running for the ball. A push is obstruction, which is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: An offside player deliberately stands in the way of an opponent who is trying to reach the ball. What is the sanction?

options.text: No sanction unless contact is made

questions.explanation: An offside player must not intentionally obstruct an opponent or interfere with play.

questions.stem: A support runner deliberately steps into the path of a defender who is about to tackle the ball-carrier. What does the referee award?

options.text: A scrum to the defending team

questions.explanation: A player must not intentionally stop an opponent from tackling, or trying to tackle, the ball-carrier.

questions.stem: A player must not intentionally deny an opponent the chance to play the ball. What is the one lawful way of doing so?

options.text: By standing still in the opponent's path
By shielding the ball from an offside position

questions.explanation: An opponent may be kept from the ball only by genuinely competing for possession.

questions.stem: A ball-carrier deliberately runs into an offside team-mate so that defenders cannot get to the ball-carrier. What is the decision?
questions.explanation: Intentionally running into an offside team-mate to obstruct the opposition is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: The ball is dead and a player holds an opponent back to stop a quick restart. Is this an offence?

options.text: Only if the opponent is hurt
Only if it happens inside a 22
Yes, opponents must not be obstructed while the ball is dead
No, obstruction applies only when the ball is in play

questions.explanation: A player must not obstruct or interfere with an opponent in any way while the ball is dead.

questions.stem: What is the sanction for obstruction?
questions.explanation: Every form of obstruction listed in the law is sanctioned with a penalty.

questions.stem: A player deliberately breaks a law to stop the opposition's attack. Under which heading of foul play does intentionally infringing fall?
questions.explanation: Intentionally infringing any law of the game is unfair play.

questions.stem: A defender under pressure deliberately bats the ball over the touchline with a hand. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Intentionally knocking, placing, pushing or throwing the ball out of the playing area with the hand or arm is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: A defender in in-goal deliberately throws the ball over the dead-ball line. What sanction does the law give?
questions.explanation: Throwing the ball from the playing area on purpose is unfair play, sanctioned with a penalty.

questions.stem: A player dives to the ground pretending to have been obstructed, hoping to win a penalty. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: A player must not do anything that might lead the officials to think an opponent has infringed.

questions.stem: What is the sanction for wasting time?
questions.explanation: Time-wasting is the one unfair play offence sanctioned with a free-kick.

questions.stem: Which of these unfair play offences is sanctioned with a free-kick instead of a penalty?

options.text: Intentionally throwing the ball into touch

questions.explanation: Wasting time carries a free-kick. The other unfair play offences carry a penalty.

questions.stem: What is the sanction when a team repeatedly commits the same offence?
questions.explanation: Repeated infringement, by a team or by a player, is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: One player keeps infringing the laws in different ways. Does the law on repeated infringements cover this?

options.text: Yes, a player must not repeatedly infringe the laws
Only if it is the same offence each time
No, only a team can be guilty of repeated infringement
Only if the offences fall within ten minutes

questions.explanation: As well as a team repeating the same offence, an individual player must not repeatedly infringe.

questions.stem: Different players in the same team keep committing the same offence. What does the referee do first?

options.text: Shows a yellow card to the latest offender
Gives a general caution to the team
Shows a yellow card to the captain

questions.explanation: The referee starts with a general caution to the whole team.

questions.stem: After a general caution for repeated infringements, the team commits the same offence again. What follows?

options.text: A yellow card for the guilty player or players
A second general caution to the team's captain
A red card for the captain of the team
A penalty try, wherever it happens on the field

questions.explanation: Once the team has been cautioned, a repeat of the offence brings a yellow card for whoever is guilty.

questions.stem: A ball-carrier runs into contact leading with the elbow. How does the law treat this?

options.text: As legal if the tackler was upright

questions.explanation: Leading with the elbow or forearm is given as an example of reckless or dangerous play.

questions.stem: A ball-carrier hurdles a defender who is bending down to make a tackle. How does the law treat jumping over a tackler?

options.text: As legal close to the try line
As legal if no contact is made

questions.explanation: Jumping into, or over, a tackler is listed as dangerous play.

questions.stem: Which of these is listed in law as physical abuse?

options.text: Shoulder-to-shoulder contact when chasing the ball
A hand-off made without excessive force

questions.explanation: Physical abuse includes biting, punching, contact with the eye area, striking, stamping, trampling, tripping and kicking.

questions.stem: Does the law on abuse cover words as well as actions?

options.text: Only words aimed at the referee
No, it covers physical acts only
Yes, it covers physical and verbal abuse

questions.explanation: The law forbids both physical and verbal abuse of anyone.

questions.stem: A player trips an opponent with a foot. How does the law classify tripping?

options.text: As a legal way to stop a ball-carrier

questions.explanation: Tripping is one of the listed forms of physical abuse.

questions.stem: A defender tackles a player well after that player has passed the ball. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: A player must not tackle an opponent late. The sanction is a penalty.

questions.stem: May a player tackle an opponent who does not have the ball?

options.text: Yes, if the opponent is within a metre of the ball
Yes, if the opponent is about to receive the ball
No, only a player in possession may be tackled
Yes, if the opponent is offside

questions.explanation: A player must not tackle an opponent who is not in possession of the ball.

questions.stem: In which phases may a player without the ball push an opponent who is also without the ball?

options.text: Any phase, if both players are onside

questions.explanation: Outside a scrum, ruck or maul, a player without the ball must not hold, push, charge or obstruct an opponent without the ball.

questions.stem: A defender shoulder-charges the ball-carrier without trying to wrap the arms. What is the decision?

options.text: Penalty, because no attempt was made to grasp the player
Play on, because the ball-carrier may be stopped by any means

questions.explanation: A player must not charge or knock down a ball-carrier without attempting to grasp that player.

questions.stem: A player jumps to catch a high kick and an opponent tackles the player while both feet are off the ground. What is the decision?
questions.explanation: A player whose feet are off the ground must not be tackled, charged, pulled, pushed or grasped.

questions.stem: An opponent is in the air catching a kick. When may that opponent be tackled?

options.text: As soon as the ball touches the hands
At any time, if the tackler has also jumped
Once the opponent's feet are back on the ground
As soon as the ball is caught

questions.explanation: No tackle may be made on a player whose feet are off the ground.

questions.stem: A tackler lifts the ball-carrier off the ground and drops the player so that the head and shoulders hit the ground first. What is the decision?

options.text: Play on if the ball is released

questions.explanation: A lifted opponent must not be dropped or driven so that the head or upper body makes contact with the ground.

questions.stem: What makes a lifting tackle illegal under the law?

options.text: Dropping or driving the lifted player so the head or upper body hits the ground
Carrying the lifted player backwards for more than a metre
Holding the lifted player in the air for more than a second
Lifting both of the player's feet off the ground at any point

questions.explanation: The offence is lifting an opponent and then dropping or driving them so that the head or upper body strikes the ground.

questions.stem: A player is punched and punches back. What does the law say about the second punch?

options.text: Only the first punch is an offence
Retaliation is excused if the first offender is sent off

questions.explanation: Retaliation is itself an offence, whatever provoked it.

questions.stem: What does the law say about the flying wedge?

options.text: It may be used only near the try line
It may be used if no more than three players bind
It may be used only from a penalty

questions.explanation: The flying wedge is banned outright.

questions.stem: What is a flying wedge?

options.text: A maul that forms after a lineout catch
Team-mates bound each side of the ball-carrier before engaging
A defensive line rushing up in an arrowhead shape
A scrum that wheels through more than 90 degrees

questions.explanation: In a flying wedge, team-mates bind on either side of the ball-carrier in a wedge before hitting the opposition.

questions.stem: A defender tries to kick the ball out of the ball-carrier's hands. What is the decision?

options.text: Play on if only the ball is kicked

questions.explanation: A player must not attempt to kick the ball from the hands of the ball-carrier.

questions.stem: Is a ball-carrier allowed to hand off an opponent?

options.text: No, a hand-off is illegal in every case
Yes, but only against an opponent who is offside
Yes, with any amount of force
Yes, provided excessive force is not used

questions.explanation: A hand-off is permitted as long as the force used is not excessive.

questions.stem: With which part of the body is a hand-off made?
questions.explanation: A hand-off is the ball-carrier fending off an opponent with the palm of the hand.

questions.stem: What is a stiff-arm tackle?

options.text: A tackle in which the tackler does not let go
A legal fend by the ball-carrier
An illegal tackle using a stiff arm to strike

questions.explanation: A stiff-arm tackle is an illegal tackle where the tackler strikes the ball-carrier with a stiff arm.

questions.stem: In open play, may a player lift or support a team-mate, for example to catch a kick-off?

options.text: Yes, any player may lift or support a team-mate
No, lifting is allowed only at a lineout
Yes, but only if the opposition also lift
Yes, but only forwards may be lifted

questions.explanation: Lifting or supporting a team-mate is permitted in open play.

questions.stem: In open play a player is lifted by a team-mate to catch a kick. What must the lifter do once the ball is won?

options.text: Let go of the player at once
Step away so the player can pass
Lower the player to the ground safely
Keep the player up until a maul forms

questions.explanation: The lifted player must be brought safely to the ground as soon as either team has won the ball.

questions.stem: A player lifted by a team-mate in open play is not lowered safely once the ball has been won. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Failing to lower a lifted team-mate safely in open play is a free-kick offence.

questions.stem: A tackler's arm makes contact with the ball-carrier's neck. How does the law treat this?

options.text: As a legal tackle if the ball is dislodged

questions.explanation: A tackle that makes contact with an opponent's head or neck is a dangerous tackle.

questions.stem: A tackle starts on the ball-carrier's chest and slides up so that the tackler's arm ends in contact with the head. Is it a dangerous tackle?

options.text: Only if the ball is lost
No, because it started in a legal position
Yes, even though it started lower
Only if the ball-carrier is hurt

questions.explanation: A tackle that ends in contact with the head or neck is dangerous even if it began lower on the body.

questions.stem: What is the sanction for a tackle that makes contact with an opponent's head or neck?

options.text: Play on if the ball stays in play

questions.explanation: Dangerous tackling is sanctioned with a penalty, and the player may also be cautioned or sent off.

questions.stem: A player clearing out a ruck makes contact with an opponent's head. What is the decision?

options.text: Penalty for dangerous play in a ruck
Play on, because contact at a ruck is unavoidable
Scrum to the team in possession

questions.explanation: In a ruck or maul a player must not make contact with an opponent's head or neck.

questions.stem: In a maul, where on an opponent's body must a player not make contact?
questions.explanation: Contact with an opponent's head or neck in a ruck or maul is dangerous play.

questions.stem: At a scrum, one front row forms up at a distance and rushes at its opponents. How does the law treat this?

options.text: As a legal engagement once "set" is called
As a matter for a free-kick only
As legal if both front rows do it
As dangerous play in a scrum

questions.explanation: A front row must not form at a distance from its opponents and rush against them.

questions.stem: A front-row player pulls an opponent in the scrum. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Pulling an opponent in the front row is dangerous play, sanctioned with a penalty.

questions.stem: A front-row player deliberately forces an opponent upwards out of the scrum. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Intentionally lifting an opponent off their feet or forcing them up out of the scrum is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: A front-row player intentionally collapses a scrum. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: Intentionally collapsing a scrum is dangerous play and a penalty offence.

questions.stem: What counts as charging into a ruck or maul?

options.text: Joining with the head lower than the hips
Any contact made without binding onto another player in it
Joining at speed, even with a bind

questions.explanation: Charging includes any contact made without binding onto a player in the ruck or maul.

questions.stem: A player hits a ruck shoulder-first without binding onto anyone. What is the decision?

options.text: Penalty for charging into a ruck

questions.explanation: Contact with a ruck or maul without binding is charging, which is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: A defender deliberately pulls down a maul. What is the sanction?

options.text: Scrum to the team in possession

questions.explanation: Intentionally collapsing a ruck or maul is a penalty offence.

questions.stem: How may a player lawfully remove a jackler from the tackle area?

options.text: By pushing or driving the jackler backwards
By twisting the jackler off the ball
By rolling the jackler to one side

questions.explanation: A jackler may be pushed or driven backwards, but must not be rolled, pulled or twisted.

questions.stem: When driving a jackler backwards out of the tackle area, may a player grab the jackler's leg?

options.text: No, the legs must not be touched
Only if the jackler is already off their feet
Yes, the knee or leg may be grabbed to drive the jackler back
Only if the jackler has hold of the ball

questions.explanation: Pushing or driving the jackler backwards is allowed, including by grabbing the knee or leg.

questions.stem: A player grips a jackler around the body and twists the jackler sideways to the ground. What is this action, and is it allowed?

options.text: A crocodile roll, which is prohibited

questions.explanation: Rolling, twisting or pulling a player who is on their feet in the tackle area to ground is a crocodile roll, and it is banned.

questions.stem: At a ruck, a player drops their body weight onto an opponent's legs. What is the decision?
questions.explanation: A player must not drop their weight onto an opponent or target the lower limbs.

questions.stem: Which part of an opponent's body must a player in a ruck or maul not target?
questions.explanation: Targeting an opponent's lower limbs in a ruck or maul is dangerous play.

questions.stem: A defender deliberately charges into a player who has just kicked the ball. What is the sanction?
questions.explanation: A player must not intentionally charge or obstruct an opponent who has just kicked the ball.

questions.stem: After a late charge on the kicker, who chooses where the penalty is taken?
questions.explanation: The non-offending team chooses between the place of the infringement and the place related to where the ball went.

questions.stem: A kicker is charged late and the ball lands in the field of play. Besides the place of the charge, where may the penalty be taken?

options.text: Ten metres on from the place of the charge
Where the ball lands or is next played
Where the kicker's team next gains possession

questions.explanation: The team may take the penalty where the ball lands or is next played, though no closer than 15 metres to touch.

questions.stem: A kicker is charged late and the ball lands two metres from the touchline. If the team takes the penalty where the ball landed, how far in from touch is it?
questions.explanation: A penalty taken where the ball lands can be no nearer than 15 metres from the touchline.
